scene.nanakusa-gayu.narrative.094e40b1:
In Japan, the Jinjitsu seasonal festival on January 7 includes the custom of eating seven-herb rice porridge and wishing for freedom from illness and misfortune. Young spring greens are added to rice porridge, and this seasonal food carries hopes for good health in the new year. Ingredients and cooking methods vary between regions and households; no single recipe is prescribed here.

Before you is a pot of vegetable porridge that has already been prepared. Move the wooden ladle into the pot and stir gently, scoop up a ladleful, then serve it into a bowl, holding a wish for the well-being of yourself and those you care about. The vessel shapes, colours, ladle rest and three stages of interaction are arrangements for this experience. It focuses on serving food, without simulating an offering or actual eating, and does not treat serving virtual porridge as producing a health benefit.
scene.brat-bride-cloth.narrative.1f2193d:
On the eve of Saint Brigid's feast day in Ireland, some people leave a piece of cloth or ribbon on an outside windowsill or by the door of their home, hoping that the saint will bless it as she passes. Known as Brat Bríde or Ribín Bríde, this cloth-leaving custom is connected with folk beliefs in protecting the family and easing illness and suffering. Recorded cloth shapes and uses differ; no particular colour or size should be treated as a universal requirement.

At dusk, a prepared square of cloth lies before you. Lift it from the wooden stool, move it outside the window and gently lay it on the sill, holding a wish for the safety of yourself and those you care about. The window frame, cloth shape, colours and continuous carrying and placement are arrangements for this experience. Laying it down now means only that the placement is complete; the night quietly continues, and the thoughts you leave are yours to cherish. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.korean-sotdae.narrative.bff5c305:
In some Korean villages, tall poles topped with wooden birds are called 솟대, or sotdae. They are erected at village entrances to express hopes for the village's protection and prayers to the sky. The wooden birds have different forms, including ducks, and associated village rites also vary locally. These poles are connected with village beliefs and should not be treated simply as ordinary wooden decorations.

Before you is a wooden bird pole that has already been prepared. Lift it from its wooden support, slowly bring it upright, then let its foot settle securely, holding a wish for the safety of home and those you care about. This presents a preparatory moment in erecting a pole; the bird shape, wooden rings, supports, socket and continuous carrying and placement are all arrangements for this experience. The foot settling means only that the placement before you is complete. May everyday life be peaceful and those you love be safe. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.japanese-kadomatsu.narrative.3e84f:
In Japanese New Year customs for welcoming deities, kadomatsu stand at a doorway or entrance as markers to welcome the deity of the year. Pine branches are accompanied by bamboo, and they may be displayed in pairs. People prepare these entrance displays with thoughts of welcoming the new year and divine favour. They are connected with belief rather than being simply ordinary potted decorations. Practices differ by location; no single form or orientation should be treated as a universal requirement.

The pine-and-bamboo kadomatsu before you is already prepared. Gently lift the straw bundle from its wooden rest, move it to the doorway on the right and slowly set it down, forming a pair with the one on the other side, and hold a wish for a peaceful new year for yourself and your family. The continuous carrying and placement, specific shapes of the straw, pine and bamboo, rope rings, wooden door and tray are arrangements for this experience. Setting the kadomatsu down means only that this placement is complete. May the days ahead be peaceful and your steps unhurried. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.pucara-rooftop-bulls.narrative.a88:
In southern Peru, clay Toritos de Pucará are connected with local beliefs in protecting the home. A pair of clay bulls is placed on a rooftop, expressing wishes for the family's protection and an abundant life. They feature clay horns, curled tails and floral ornaments, and also have a history as ritual vessels associated with Pachamama and livestock-marking rites. The rooftop display is the moment selected here; differing household and artisan practices are not reduced to one exclusive rule.

A prepared pair of clay bulls stands before you. Lift the wooden board beneath them, move it above the roof ridge and gently set it down, holding a wish for the safety of the family you care about. The bulls' specific forms, colours and flowers, the board, house shape and supporting platform are designs for this experience. The continuous dragging, their paths and duration are also product arrangements. Completing the placement means only that the clay bulls before you have been set down. May home be peaceful and life abundant. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.chinese-longevity-lock.narrative.5:
A longevity lock is a lock-shaped neck ornament carrying wishes for safety, good fortune and long life. Some museum examples are made of silver with a necklace and dangling floral ornaments; other lock plaques are worn on cotton cords. The practice of putting one on a child has carried beliefs in locking life in place and seeking protection, with a genuine religious background. Wearers are not limited to children, and no single form or set of practices should be treated as a universal rule everywhere.

The silver lock and cotton neck cord before you are already prepared. Gently lift the supporting board, move it above the gift box and slowly set it down, holding a wish for a child to grow up safely. The curved lock plaque, orange neck cord and small flower pendants are an original combination based on documented object features. The specific lettering, colours, number of flowers, board, gift box and continuous carrying and placement are arrangements for this experience. Finishing the packing means only that the lock ornament before you has been placed; it does not mean that wearing it, a blessing rite or actual protection has been completed. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.uchide-wishing-mallet.narrative.31:
The uchide no kozuchi is connected with Japanese legends of good fortune and wishes. In a record of one Setsubun event, Imizu Shrine described family members gently shaking a little mallet with wishes, explaining it as a treasure to shake while holding a wish. The magical power in the tale of Issun-bōshi belongs to legend. This experience retains its religious and storytelling background, without presenting shaking the mallet as a method that is certain to grant wishes in reality or treating one event as a universal ritual sequence.

The small mallet before you already rests on a wooden stand. Gently lift its handle, shake it in the air and return it to its place, holding a blessing for what you hope for. The red-lacquered wood, golden edging, tassel at the handle end and double support are an original design for this experience. The three drags and this shake's direction, range and duration are also product arrangements. Setting the mallet down means only that the visible action is complete. May your hopes find new progress, and may your steps forward be steady.
At Alasita in La Paz, Bolivia, people obtain miniatures representing things they wish for, and houses are one such category. These objects are connected with belief in Ekeko, the Aymara deity of abundance. Real-world practices also include consecration by Andean ritual practitioners or blessings by Catholic priests. Participants entrust their hopes for life to these little objects.

Before you is a miniature house with an original design. Lift it, turn it to look at its doors, windows and roof, then place it on a cushion while thinking about the home you hope for. This focuses on the moment of choosing an object of aspiration. The house design, colours, cushion and continuous carrying and placement are arrangements for this experience; they do not represent a fixed ritual sequence or replace a real-world blessing. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.yusheng-lohei.narrative.dd662bad:
At Lunar New Year meals in Singapore, a large platter of yusheng often brings relatives, friends and colleagues together. Slices of fish and colourful ingredients such as shredded radish are arranged on the platter. Once sauce is added, everyone reaches in with chopsticks to toss and mix the food together, exchanging auspicious New Year greetings as they do. This shared tossing is called lohei and is now also part of family reunions and company New Year meals.

Ingredients and combinations vary between households and restaurants. Here, the shared tossing moment is presented as a colourful platter of fish slices, shredded vegetables and crisp pieces. Chopsticks lift the ingredients into the air and gently return them to the platter, gradually weaving together colours that were separate. Offer a wish for an abundant new year and good things for family and friends to those gathered around the table now.
scene.kitano-nadeushi.narrative.360b37d2:
Several reclining ox statues stand in the grounds of Kitano Tenmangū in Kyoto. The shrine regards the ox as a messenger of Tenjin, Sugawara no Michizane, and describes the belief in gently stroking the ox's head while praying for success in learning. This intention is connected with students' respect for Tenjin.

Here is a reclining stone ox with an original design. Bring the palm towards its forehead, gently stroke it and slowly withdraw the hand, holding a wish for your studies to go well. The stone ox rests quietly on its base as the palm follows the curve of its forehead and finally returns in front of you. You can keep the lessons and examinations you are preparing for in mind.
scene.lao-baci-wrist.narrative.ff09f8da:
In Luang Prabang, Laos, Baci, also called Sou Khuan, is a ceremony for blessing relatives and friends at important moments in life. When someone leaves on a journey, returns after a long absence or celebrates a happy life event, people may gather to tie white threads around the recipient's wrist, speaking wishes as they knot them. The white cotton thread makes care between people visible. It carries hopes for the safety and good fortune of the person before them.

Baci also has a religious background of calling back khuan. It is led by community elders familiar with the ceremony, and participants also share a meal afterwards. Its meaning exists within the gathering of family and community. This experience focuses on the wrist-tying moment of welcoming a relative or friend home: pick up a strand of white cotton, wrap it around the outstretched wrist and gently draw the knot closed, leaving a wish close by with the thread.
scene.finnish-virpominen.narrative.06e7c:
In one form of Easter neighbourhood visiting in present-day Espoo, Finland, children first obtain the host's permission, then wave decorated pussy-willow branches and recite wishes for health and good fortune. The children give the branches to the host, who places sweets such as chocolate eggs into the visitors' basket in thanks. The people visited, costumes and timing of thank-you gifts differ between communities.

The willow branch before you is already decorated. Gently wave it, offer these good wishes and receive the thank-you gift the host places in the basket. The paper flowers, little entrance scene and three actions are original storyboards arranged for this experience. They capture a moment of exchanging blessings rather than representing a fixed ritual sequence shared everywhere.
scene.scottish-first-footing.narrative.2:
In Scotland's Hogmanay New Year customs, first-footing is a New Year visit centred on the first person to enter a home after midnight. The visitor brings gifts for the household, and coal is one documented gift. Connected with the warmth of the hearth, it carries wishes for a warm home and a good life in the new year. Specific gifts and participation practices vary by place and period; they should not be reduced to one identical set of rules everywhere.

Here you visit this household with a gift of coal as the first guest after New Year's midnight. Pick up the coal you have brought, carry it through the open doorway and place it in the host's hearth, leaving wishes for warmth and well-being in the new year with this family. You can turn the coal in your hand to inspect it, then carry it continuously through the open doorway and into the hearth from the front.
scene.hiiragi-iwashi.narrative.6fdbdd93:
One Japanese doorway arrangement around Setsubun combines a roasted sardine head with a hiiragi branch and is called hiiragi iwashi. In folk explanations, the prickly leaf edges and the fish head's smell are regarded as things that frighten demons away. They are therefore placed at entrances with wishes to ward off misfortune and protect the home. This seemingly simple combination of materials has an explicit context of the threshold and driving away evil.

Muramatsu Kokuzōdō in Ibaraki Prefecture still introduces this Setsubun practice, and the Japan Toy Museum in Himeji, Hyōgo Prefecture, has also documented actual entrance displays of roasted fish heads and hiiragi branches. Different places have their own practices for putting them up and taking them down; these local practices together form the doorway scenes of Setsubun. Here, pick up the prepared branch, fit it to the roasted fish head and place it beside the door, presenting a short moment of preparing a doorway decoration.
scene.tamagushi-offering.narrative.18605:
A tamagushi is a branch offering placed before the kami in prayers and festivals at Japanese shrines, usually made from a fresh sakaki branch with shide paper streamers and other materials attached. According to the Association of Shinto Shrines, worshippers entrust sincerity and prayers to the tamagushi and then offer it to the deity. The branch becomes a medium for expressing respect and seeking divine favour between people and kami. Its meaning is connected with the religious occasion, rather than being simply a branch with added decoration.

Public instructions for offering include supporting the branch with both hands, turning its orientation, concentrating on one's prayer, then placing it on the offering table with its base towards the deity. The orientation and careful holding of the branch give an inner prayer a tangible form in a carefully tended offering. What you see retains a section after taking up the branch: straighten the sakaki, pray quietly, then turn towards the offering table and gently set it down.
scene.tibetan-water-bowls.narrative.74ee:
Offering water is a Tibetan Buddhist practice of expressing respect to Buddhas and bodhisattvas with clear water, also taught publicly today by Buddhist centres abroad. Water may appear ordinary, but offering it requires care: the bowls first contain a little water, and water is poured gently without overflowing. Cleaning the vessels and arranging the offerings are connected with approaching those to whom they are offered with respect.

In relevant teachings from 1998, Lama Zopa Rinpoche placed the motivation in wishing that all sentient beings be free from suffering and move towards awakening, with dedication at the end. Water offerings are not simply an exchange for personal health or wealth. Seven copper bowls are already arranged before the Buddha image in this scene. Lift the jug, add water to each bowl from left to right, then put the jug back, retaining this small part of the offering process.
scene.kagami-biraki-sake.narrative.51bf1:
The "mirror" in Japan's sake kagami-biraki ceremony refers to the round wooden lid of a sake barrel. People use wooden mallets to open a lid that has already been loosened, joining in wishes for a smooth new beginning at weddings, business openings, the completion of buildings and commemorative celebrations. The word "opening" in its name also carries an auspicious sense of opening a path ahead and moving towards fulfilment.

Gekkeikan's account places kagami-biraki within Japan's cultural background of offering sake to the deities, praying, and then sharing food and drink; celebrations today can take different forms. The straw matting, or komo, around the barrel originally helped protect wooden barrels during transport in the Edo period and later also became part of their festive decoration. The lid before you has already been loosened. Pick up the mallet with its red and white ribbons, gently strike one end of the seam, then put the mallet away, experiencing just this brief part of opening the lid.
scene.tibetan-prayer-flags.narrative.796:
Prayer flags are part of Tibetan Buddhist life in Tibet and the Himalayan region, and Tibetan monasteries and communities overseas continue to make them. Printed with prayers or mantras, the flags hang outdoors where the wind can pass through them. According to a Tibetan nuns' organisation, the intention when hanging them should extend to all beings, with the hope that compassion, peace and goodwill will spread with the wind, rather than seeking only personal benefit for the person hanging them.

In this account by the Tibetan nuns' organisation, the linked blue, white, red, green and yellow flags are associated respectively with sky, air, fire, water and earth. Their gradual fading also reminds people of change and impermanence. Prayer flags should therefore be treated respectfully. Pick up each end of the string of flags in turn and carry it directly to its elevated hanging point, spreading out the flags so the five colours unfold in the wind.
scene.rosh-hashanah-apple-honey.narrativ:
Dipping apples in honey is a custom at the festive table for Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year. Sweetness is joined with prayer: blessing the fruit, tasting the apple and honey, and asking God for a good and sweet year. Chabad's account of the custom cites a reference to apples in medieval French rabbinic writing. From those older texts to family tables today, fruit and sweetness have carried hopes for the new year.

Festive food gives an abstract wish a taste that can be shared, bringing hopes for the new year into a family meal. The sweetness expresses a prayer addressed to God, and the encounter between people and food also becomes part of festive memory. Here you experience just the dipping: pick up a prepared apple slice, dip it in honey, then lift it and return it to the plate, ready to be tasted.
scene.thai-songkran-elders.narrative.af7:
Songkran is Thailand's New Year festival, in which family reunions and respect for elders have an important place. Many people know its lively water-splashing celebrations, but among relatives and elders there is also the quieter Rod Nam Dum Hua. Younger people pour clear or scented water over an elder's hands to show respect and ask for their blessing for the new year. The water is associated with welcoming the year and an intention of purification.

An overseas celebration documented by Thailand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 2016 also included pouring water for elders, showing how these family and intergenerational relationships continue in communities abroad. Details of etiquette vary between families and places, while the gentle act of pouring preserves respect for elders. Lift the small bowl, move it towards the elder's hands and slowly pour the water, then gently set the bowl down again. Carrying can be one continuous motion; while holding it level, you can also turn it horizontally to take a closer look.
scene.kameido-usokae.narrative.7bdabeb7:
Kameido Tenjin Shrine in Tokyo's Koto ward holds its Usokae observance on January 24 and 25 each year. Visitors return the previous year's wooden bullfinch to the shrine and receive a new one, praying for misfortune to turn to good fortune. In Japanese, the bird's name, uso, sounds the same as the word for a lie. Through this connection, people hope that past troubles may become as though they had never been real, and welcome the year with renewed intentions.

Tokyo's official tourism information dates this observance at Kameido Tenjin Shrine to 1820. It is part of local Tenjin worship, within the context of a shrine dedicated to Sugawara no Michizane. Though the carved wooden bird has an appealing appearance, it is more than an ordinary toy. Return the old bird, receive a new one and place it carefully, preserving the relationship between returning and receiving, with a prayer for misfortune to become good fortune held between the wooden birds. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.persian-esfand.narrative.70de3fa3:
Burning esfand seeds is a folk practice for averting harm in Iran and in some Iranian households overseas. The plant used is Syrian rue. People believe that the smoke rising from its seeds can ward off the evil eye and protect their family and home. Encyclopaedia Iranica notes that burning the seeds against the evil eye appears in early classical Persian literature. This belief in smoke and protection also continues in the living memories of some families.

An oral account from an Iranian American family, collected in 2021, specifically describes a grandmother heating the seeds in a pan on the stove, then waving a cloth to spread the smoke, particularly when she feared that things were going badly at home. Here you experience a moment from that family memory: lift the pan onto the stove, wait for the smoke to rise, then gently wave the cloth, expressing a wish to avert harm and protect the home. Carrying can be one continuous motion; while holding it level, you can also turn it horizontally to take a closer look.
scene.mochigase-nagashibina.narrative.a2:
In the nagashibina custom of Mochigase in Tottori, Japan, a pair of paper hina dolls are placed on a round straw support with a peach branch and sweets, then released into a gentle stretch of the Sendai River on the third day of the third lunar month. Here the paper dolls are katashiro, substitutes that receive a person's misfortune and impurity. Sending them away on the water expresses prayers for freedom from illness and calamity and for children to grow up safely.

This practice was once passed down in many places in the Inaba region, and Mochigase still preserves a distinctive local form. The earlier practice of individual households releasing them in the evening has also developed into activities with times arranged collectively by the community. The tradition retains its meaning of purification from misfortune while changing with the ways people take part. Lift the prepared paper dolls, flowering branch and straw support, move them over the gentle current and softly lower them into the water, watching this group of offerings drift away. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.greek-vasilopita.narrative.e8fb4bc:
Vasilopita means "Saint Basil's bread" and is shared at New Year in Greek Orthodox families and churches. Recipes vary by place: some make a sweet bread, others a cake. One striking detail they share is a coin hidden inside, with the person receiving the portion containing it believed to receive a blessing. It carries hopes for health and happiness as the new year begins.

Holy Cross Greek Orthodox Church's account of the custom also connects it with the memory of Saint Basil's charity: a portion is set aside for people in need when the cake is divided, so that a family's celebration includes care for others. Church stories about Saint Basil give this New Year food a meaning of caring for the poor. Move an already-cut portion onto a family member's plate, then take out the coin that is revealed, holding onto a moment of sharing food in the new year. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.tibetan-khata-greeting.narrative.6:
The khata is a ceremonial scarf used to express respect in Tibetan social and religious life. Today it is also found in communities in Nepal, Bhutan and parts of the Indian Himalayas. When welcoming guests, seeing off family or friends, or expressing thanks, people offer the scarf, placing feelings beyond words into another person's hands. Its use varies with the recipient and occasion; the etiquette for welcoming an ordinary guest is not exactly the same as that for honouring a religious teacher.

A white khata is often understood to express purity, sincerity and goodwill, and is carefully folded and respectfully supported when offered. The soft scarf connects arrivals and departures, giving visible form to welcome, gratitude or good wishes. Before you is simply a modest welcome for a guest: lift the folded white silk with both hands, offer it towards the visitor and let them take it securely. Carrying can be one continuous motion; while holding it level, you can also turn it horizontally to take a closer look.
Shichi-Go-San is a Japanese celebration of children's growth, usually centred on ages three, five and seven and shrine visits around November 15. Kanagawa Prefecture's cultural introduction notes that customs of this kind spread through the Kanto region during the Edo period, later extending to Kyoto, Osaka and other places. Families mark their children's gradual growth through the festival and express hopes for health and long life.

Chitose ame is a common gift at this celebration. Long, slender red and white sweets are placed in an elongated bag. Both the name, meaning "thousand-year candy", and the long shape express the hope that children will enjoy lasting health and well-being. The bags' decorations take many forms today. Here is a moment in which a parent gives the gift to a child: grasp the bag's handles, bring it closer and slowly lower it so that the child can take it securely. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.mongolian-ovoo.narrative.fd29227d:
In Mongolia, ovoos are sacred markers, often made of piled stones and sometimes incorporating branches and ceremonial scarves, found near mountains or significant waters. They are connected with people's reverence and respect for mountains and rivers. Visitors add stones and make offerings, allowing the ovoo to grow, and through this ask mountains and lakes for protection.

Anthropologist Kip Hutchins's fieldwork in Mongolia records one common approach: quietly making three clockwise circuits, picking up stones from the ground and adding them to the pile. However, different ovoos vary in purpose, offerings and local understandings, so this practice cannot be treated as the only procedure. Pick up the stone, follow the visitor's circuit and add it to the ovoo, preserving the connection between walking, adding stones, and honouring the mountains while praying for protection.
scene.fgs-buddha-bathing.narrative.ddba2:
Bathing the Buddha on his birthday involves pouring fragrant water over a statue of the infant prince, expressing remembrance, reverence and gratitude for the birth of Shakyamuni Buddha. Fo Guang Shan's public explanation relates the practice to the Buddhist birth story: after the prince was born, he pointed towards heaven and earth, and streams of water descended from the sky to bathe him. Devotees bathe the statue to commemorate this birth story and honour the compassion and wisdom taught by the Buddha.

In Yilan, Taiwan, the Buddha's birthday celebrations organised by Master Hsing Yun from 1954 included bathing the Buddha, processions and chanting the Buddha's name. Fo Guang Shan's explanation also emphasises purifying greed, anger and delusion, and body, speech and mind, while extending care through good deeds to all beings. Following that organisation's public steps, pour three ladles of water over the infant prince's right shoulder, left shoulder and right shoulder, respectively vowing to stop evil, do good and liberate sentient beings. This offers an introduction to the connection between reverence and the resolve to practise.
scene.balinese-canang-sari.narrative.12d:
In Bali, Indonesia, canang sari are offerings used daily by Balinese Hindus, found in homes, temples, at crossroads and at offering places beside fields. Flowers and other offerings are arranged in a tray made from leaves, expressing gratitude to Ida Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa and prayers for peace and harmony in life.

An explanation from a Balinese Hindu organisation places importance on sincerity when preparing and presenting the offering, and explains the religious meaning of the flower colours, directions and components such as the porosan in the tray. The materials and arrangement give gratitude and prayer a form that can be prepared by hand and solemnly offered, connecting daily preparation with religious life. Most offerings in the leaf tray before you are already prepared. Add the white flower, lift the tray and place it on the offering platform beside the field, becoming acquainted with this small part of a daily offering. After adding the flower, carry and place the tray in one continuous motion, keeping its orientation.
scene.bulgarian-survakane.narrative.197e:
In the Bulgarian New Year custom of Survakane, children hold a decorated cornel branch called a survachka, gently tap relatives and friends on the back and recite wishes for health and happiness in the coming year. It takes place during New Year visits between people, with the branch, spoken wishes and gathering together forming this moment of welcome for the year.

The Regional Historical Museum in Burgas records that cornel is associated in local folklore with strength and longevity. Branches may be wrapped with woollen thread and strung with popcorn, dried fruit or other decorations; local materials also reflect different ways of life and production. The greetings between family and friends and the decorations on the branch give visible, participatory form to hopes for the new year. The coloured branch before you is already decorated. Lift it, move it behind your relative or friend, gently tap their back and draw it away, offering a wish for good health to someone close to you. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.lanna-sand-pagoda.narrative.2b68d2:
The Lanna New Year in northern Thailand is called Pi Mai Mueang. During the festival, people bring sand to temples and build sand pagodas as an act of Buddhist merit-making, decorating them with long banners called tung made from coloured paper and bamboo poles. The Thailand Foundation's account also records a local belief that these banners draw the souls of the dead out of hell, giving the offering of banners a religious background.

A report by Thailand's Public Relations Department on temple New Year activities in Nan also lists placing banners and offering sand pagodas. Celebrations differ between places, so the number, style and placement of banners cannot be generalised. Here you experience a brief part of decorating a sand pagoda: pick up the prepared paper and bamboo banner, move it beside the completed sand pagoda and plant the bamboo pole securely in the sand base, holding an intention of making merit for the new year. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.chinese-fu-paper.narrative.c92826f:
At Lunar New Year, people paste the character fu, meaning good fortune, on their front doors and elsewhere, expressing hopes of welcoming blessings, a happy life and a smooth future. The Taiwan Historica folklore dictionary includes fu among auspicious characters used to pray for blessings and good fortune. Introductions by the Shanghai Municipal Government and the Confucius Institute for Scotland at the University of Edinburgh also directly describe putting fu on doors and windows at New Year.

Ways of positioning fu vary from place to place. Here an upright fu character has been chosen, with the red paper prepared and resting on a small stand. The front door is nearby, its wooden panel waiting for this bright touch of red. Gently lift the paper from its stand, move it steadily to the door, then press it securely into place above. This brief experience at the doorway gives the intention of welcoming spring and good fortune a place you can arrange with your own hands. May your family be safe and the new year go smoothly, and may every homecoming remind you of this hope for life. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.turkish-nazar-bead.narrative.9a936:
In Türkiye, the nazar boncuğu is a glass protective bead with an eye-shaped design. People wear it or place it somewhere visible, expressing a wish to ward off the evil eye and protect themselves and their loved ones. This folk background of protection is retained here. Türkiye's Ministry of Culture and Tourism describes the belief, while a guide to the Ethnography Museum in Izmir explains the common combination of blue glass with white and blue circles inside.

The blue bead before you is ready, with dark blue, white and light blue around a black centre, and light gliding over its rounded glass edge. First lift it from the small ceramic support, move it steadily towards the wooden stand beside it, then let its metal loop settle gently onto the crossbar. The stand and continuous carrying and placement are arrangements for this placement experience. As the bead hangs in a visible place, hold a wish for everyday protection. May you and those you love be safe and well. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.japanese-hamaya.narrative.e5d56933:
Hamaya are decorative arrow-shaped objects of prayer and protection offered by Japanese shrines, carrying wishes to avert misfortune and find peace. The Association of Shinto Shrines describes placing them in a clean location such as a household shrine or tokonoma alcove. A notice from Tanashi Shrine also connects receiving hamaya with New Year prayers for freedom from illness and calamity and for household safety. This Shinto background of prayer and protection is retained here; placing the arrow does not mean that protection has taken effect.

Before you is a prepared decorative wooden arrow. Cream-white feathers spread along its shaft, and a red ribbon holds a small bell. Lift it from the low wooden support, move it steadily above the two supports behind it, then let the shaft settle gently into place. The particular feather shape, colours, wooden display stand and continuous carrying and placement are arrangements for this experience. The direction of movement on the screen is also not a direction prescribed by religious etiquette. With the arrow carefully placed, hold a wish for peace at home. May those you love be safe and well. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.vietnamese-five-fruit-tray.narrati:
In preparations for ancestor worship at Tết, the Vietnamese New Year, the five-fruit tray expresses gratitude to ancestors and the earth deity, along with prayers for peace, health and abundance in the new year. Fruits vary with region, season and family choice; the name "five-fruit" does not mean that each tray must contain only five varieties. Green bananas, pomelo, orange, green apple and pear are among the fruits mentioned in the relevant accounts.

Here you arrange a tray of prepared fruit. The group of green bananas and the pomelo are already on the vermilion wooden tray. Move the orange, green apple and pear from the preparation board on the left into the empty spaces one after another, watching their colours and outlines come together. The low, spread-out arrangement, particular proportions and three brief actions are arrangements for this preparation experience, differing from the familiar layered arrangement in which bananas support a pomelo. Once the tray is ready, hold a wish of gratitude and peace for the new year. May those you love share a life of health and companionship.
scene.chinese-ruyi-scepter.narrative.185:
The name ruyi conveys a good wish for things to go as desired. Relevant museum collection descriptions associate cloud-headed ruyi sceptres with auspicious charms, gifts conveying good wishes and display. Museum examples use different materials, including jade. This background of expressing good wishes is retained here, without representing the completion of a particular religious rite or promising effects in real life.

Before you is a green-jade-coloured ruyi with a cloud-shaped head and curved handle. Lift it from the preparation support, bring it towards the wooden stand on the right and set it down gently. The cloud-shaped curves, particular dimensions, material colours, two-part wooden support, courtyard and continuous carrying and placement are all arrangements for this display experience. They do not reproduce a particular museum object or prescribe a universal etiquette. Place a good wish here: may your heart have a direction, your days go smoothly and your hopes gradually come true. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.japanese-kumade.narrative.0f8d7181:
Decorative kumade rakes are regarded in Japan as auspicious objects for welcoming good fortune and praying for business prosperity. Shrine explanations connect them with the wish to rake in good fortune and with belief in the protection of Shinto and Buddhist deities. Some also come with a base for display at home. Decorations vary between places and makers. The wishes for good fortune and success in work are retained here, without representing an actual shrine bestowal or the efficacy of prayer.

The bamboo-coloured, fan-shaped kumade before you already stands on a wooden base. Bring the three gold oval paper ornaments from the preparation rack on the left, one at a time, and place them on the left and right sides of the rake and above the handle. The seven tines, three ornaments, gold paper shapes, connecting surfaces, wooden base, courtyard and three brief drags are arrangements for this decorating experience, rather than a universal religious procedure. May good fortune stay with you and your endeavours move smoothly forward.
scene.neapolitan-cornicello.narrative.a7:
The horn-shaped cornicello amulet is connected with Neapolitan beliefs in good luck and protection from the evil eye. There is also a tradition of giving it as a gift to convey good wishes. Materials and forms vary; this red horn retains a curved, pointed outline.

Place the horn on the left and the greeting card on the right inside the open gift box, then gently move the box forwards, ready to give to someone you care about. This gift preparation uses an original card and box, giving a wish for safety and well-being somewhere to rest.
scene.spanish-twelve-grapes.narrative.c2:
In Spain, the twelve grapes of New Year's Eve carry hopes for good luck and prosperity. At midnight on December 31, people eat one grape with each of twelve chimes, welcoming the new year with family and friends. The chimes at Madrid's Puerta del Sol are an iconic setting for this custom.

Before you is a moment of preparation before the chimes: place three plates of grapes on the table one after another, with four grapes on each, making twelve in all. Dividing them among three ceramic plates and using a stationary little square clock are arrangements for this experience. Here the anticipation of the new year rests in the prepared plates. Quietly await the chimes. May the new year go smoothly and good wishes stay with you.
scene.horseshoe-doorway-luck.narrative.0:
People have placed beliefs in good luck and household protection in horseshoes. In its introduction to folk magic objects from the British Isles, the Horniman Museum discusses iron and lucky horseshoes in relation to protecting the home. In a family oral account recorded by Dartmouth in 2020, an interviewee from Kentucky said that his grandmother and mother taught him to hang a horseshoe above the door with its open end upwards, hoping to keep good luck in the home.

The small doorway frame before you holds this good wish for the home. Lift, move and securely hang three iron-coloured horseshoes one at a time. The number three, the four-hole design, mounting pegs and three operations are arrangements for this experience. With the horseshoes hanging in place, may your comings and goings be safe, and may there often be good news at home.
scene.setsubun-mamemaki.narrative.531d06:
Setsubun originally marked seasonal transitions in the Japanese calendar. The familiar bean-throwing activities today are mostly held before the beginning of spring. Families put roasted soybeans in a wooden masu box and throw them outside and inside the house, calling "Demons out, good fortune in!" In this folk belief, the beans help drive away calamity. Through them, people pray for their family's well-being and a smooth life as they welcome the approaching spring.

The actions and words of Setsubun draw a clear distinction between outside and inside, and give families a way to express hopes for a new season together. Activities have their own local features, while the date of Setsubun is determined by the beginning-of-spring solar term in the calendar. First push open the wooden shutter, then gently scatter beans outwards and inwards, keeping a moment of welcoming spring at the doorway.
scene.sternsinger-house-blessing.narrati:
In Germany, Sternsinger, or "star singers", are seen during the Christmas season and at the start of the year. Children and young people visit homes to offer a Christian blessing and raise funds for aid projects supporting children in other regions. Catholic parishes are important organisers, with participants from other denominations and different backgrounds also taking part. "Children helping children" connects these doorstep visits with practical social care.

The C+M+B above the doorway comes from the Latin Christus mansionem benedicat, meaning "May Christ bless this house", with the digits on either side forming the current year. The chalk inscription thus records the visit and leaves the blessing at the entrance to the home. Pick up the chalk and write the year and letters, letting this blessing for the house gradually appear above the door.
scene.lam-tsuen-wishing-tree.narrative.c:
The wishing trees at Fong Ma Po in Lam Tsuen, Tai Po, Hong Kong, are a place to entrust wishes during Lunar New Year. Visitors write a wish on a bao die wish paper, tie it to an orange and throw it towards the branches, hoping that the paper and orange will catch and hang there. Trees near doorways and temples are connected with people's prayers, making a written sheet of paper an offering carrying personal concerns.

The custom has also changed with efforts to protect the trees. Throwing and hanging were restricted after a branch broke in 2005. By 2010, an artificial wishing tree and plastic oranges had become a way to continue the custom. New objects carry people's wishes while coexisting with the need to protect the old trees. Write the example wish "peace and safety", tie the wish paper to the plastic orange and gently throw it into the branches, experiencing the act of wishing in its current form.
scene.kagami-mochi-offering.narrative.5d:
Kagami mochi are offerings prepared during the Japanese New Year to welcome the toshigami, the deity of the year. Two flattened round rice cakes, one large and one small, are stacked together, often topped with a daidai bitter orange. Its name sounds like the word for "generation after generation", expressing hopes for the family's continuation and prosperity through the generations. The round cakes and fruit are therefore more than festive decorations; they belong within the relationship of making offerings and welcoming the new year.

In its introduction to kagami mochi, Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries presents an account tracing these offerings to the Muromachi period and explains the association between stacked round cakes and welcoming good fortune. Additional decorations and household practices still differ by region. Preparing kagami mochi and taking them down to eat after the festival are connected but distinct stages. Place the large round cake on the paper, stack the small one on top and add the orange, pausing at the moment of preparing an offering to welcome the year.
scene.romanian-martisor.narrative.168d1e:
Romanian Mărțișor brings together red and white threads twisted into a cord, given and worn in early March to welcome spring. Nineteenth-century accounts compiled by the Museum of the Romanian Peasant already describe the cords, coins and ways of wearing them. This small object has many local forms: where it is worn, the ornaments paired with it and the stories of welcoming spring vary by community. Today the spring cord may be very simple or accompanied by a small ornament.

Earlier records associate wearing the spring cord with health and good luck, but who wears it and when it is removed differ between places. In some places, the removed cord is hung on a flowering branch, bringing a person's wishes for spring alongside the growth of plants. The red and white cord before you has finished being worn. Gently lift its loop, slip it onto the flowering branch and settle the tassel, leaving this strand of spring among the flowers. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.sumiyoshi-godairiki.narrative.604b:
At Goshogozen in Sumiyoshi Taisha, Osaka, Japan, there is a custom of searching for stones bearing the characters for "five", "great" and "power". Worshippers find the three inscriptions among the small stones and put them in an omamori pouch, entrusting their wishes to the deities. The shrine's current explanation interprets the "five great powers" as physical strength, intelligence, financial strength, good fortune and longevity. Collecting the stones is connected with belief in praying for these powers.

When a wish has come true, devotees also return to express gratitude and give back the stones according to the shrine's instructions. The inscribed stones are thus both objects of prayer carried with a person and a connection between two visits. Searching, carrying them for protection and giving thanks later are all connected with people's hopes for divine protection. Pick up the three inscribed stones from among the pale pebbles one by one and place them in the open cloth pouch, keeping your wish in your heart.
scene.polish-oplatek-sharing.narrative.5:
Opłatek is a thin wafer shared by Polish families on Christmas Eve, made mainly from flour and water. The family customs of the Wigilia supper often begin as the sky darkens and the first star appears, recalling Bethlehem. After prayers and a Gospel reading, relatives share the wafer with one another and speak their good wishes. Today this family tradition also continues in Polish Catholic parishes in places such as Canada.

The piece shared is small, but the care it expresses is concrete: wishes for a family's health and safety, a willingness to forgive one another, and the sharing of joy and what life provides. It gives the night of reunion a moment for expressing reconciliation face to face. Here you experience one exchange of wishes: offer the wafer, break off a corner and let the other person receive this expression of care.
scene.greek-new-year-pomegranate.narrati:
In the New Year's Day customs of some Greek families, the year begins with a pomegranate at the front door. People smash it against the threshold, splitting its skin and scattering its red seeds to express hopes for good luck, abundance and family happiness. In its introduction to contemporary Christmas and New Year life, the Greek National Tourism Organisation still lists this act at the doorway as a New Year custom.

Here the pomegranate is both food and a bearer of wishes for the new year. The broken fruit reveals its plentiful seeds, giving visible form to the hope for abundance. The doorway, a place passed through every day, becomes a setting for seeing out the old and welcoming the new, connecting hopes for the year with family life. Pick up the whole pomegranate, move it above the stone threshold and drop it to break it open, scattering red seeds before the door. Carrying and placing can be one continuous motion; you can also turn the object freely to inspect it before placing it.
scene.bonfim-ribbon.narrative.2f106291:
The Bonfim ribbons of Salvador, in Brazil's state of Bahia, are connected with the religious life of the Senhor do Bonfim church. The city's cultural and tourism information explains that people today tie ribbons around wrists or ankles, or onto the church railings, entrusting three wishes to three knots. The ribbon is thus both something carried on the body and a way to express faith and hope.

Its form has changed over time. The nineteenth-century medida was wider and longer, made from silk or cotton, and was worn around the neck. From the mid-twentieth century onwards, the ribbon gradually became a more widely circulating souvenir. From an offering at the neck to a ribbon on the railings, changes in materials and ways of wearing it have also left traces of religious life and the city's memory. The ribbon before you is already looped around the railing. Tighten its three loose knots one after another, keeping your wishes in your heart, and watch it hang gently in the sunlight.
scene.chinowa-kuguri.narrative.69653c97:
The Nagoshi no Oharae at Japanese shrines is connected with religious practices of purification at midyear and prayers for peace. In its explanation for June 30, Kasai Shrine in Tokyo links the sins and impurities people accumulate unknowingly with prayers for freedom from illness and calamity in the next six months. Passing through a ring woven from grasses is one of the practices the shrine publicly describes.

The route recorded by Kasai Shrine passes through the ring from the front, circling back to the left, then right, then left, before continuing to the main sanctuary. This circuit, together with human-shaped figures, verses and the reverence that follows, forms the local arrangement for Nagoshi. Purification finds expression in these specific actions and prayers. The grass ring before you is ready. Slowly pass through in alternating left and right directions, finally stopping before the ring, to learn about the wishes for peace held in summer's purification.
scene.zeniarai-coin-washing.narrative.0f:
Zeniarai Benzaiten Ugafuku Shrine in Kamakura, Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, is known for the visitor custom of washing money in spring water. Coins are placed in a sieve and water is poured over them with a ladle, an act people associate with prayers for financial good fortune. In a 2025 interview, a shrine representative still described in detail the practices of worshipping, borrowing a sieve, washing money and drying it, showing how they continue in shrine life today.

The washing described in the interview takes place after worship. Washed money may be dried with a handkerchief and returned to a wallet. Handling the objects and praying to the deities belong to the same context. The coins before you are already in a shallow sieve. Lift the water ladle, let spring water flow across their surfaces and gently wipe away the droplets. The ladle returns beside the spring, leaving a small patch of clear metallic gleam.
scene.udo-undama.narrative.4e2a940a:
Udo Jingu stands on the Nichinan coast of Miyazaki Prefecture, Japan. Visitors throw small undama, or "fortune balls", towards a hollow in the back of Turtle Rock, entrusting a wish to the throw. The shrine's historical account explains that people previously threw coins. Concern for the safety of children collecting coins near the rocks later led shrine staff and a local school to replace them with clay balls, around Showa 29, or approximately 1954.

Undama are made by rolling clay into balls, pressing in the character for "fortune" and lightly firing them. Their making has also been connected with activities at schools and local organisations. The prayer cast towards Turtle Rock thus has a story rooted in modern local life. Pick up the clay ball and carry it continuously to the throwing position, turning it for a closer look first if you wish. When ready, make a separate gentle push and release to throw it. Watch it follow the on-screen arc towards the rock hollow, leaving your wish in the sea breeze.
scene.japanese-daruma-otoshi.narrative.4:
Daruma otoshi is a Japanese wooden toy: a Daruma figure stands on a stack of round wooden pieces, and the player quickly knocks out a lower piece with a small mallet while trying to keep the upper parts standing. The Edo-Tokyo Museum holds examples from the mid-twentieth century, the Showa 30s, showing that this game of stacking and striking was already part of life at that time.

The Daruma figure on top is connected with Japan's tradition of depicting Bodhidharma, the patriarch of Zen Buddhism. Its red colour, beard and rounded body make it easy to recognise. But the rules of daruma otoshi concern movement and balance, with a different context from painting the eyes of a wishing Daruma. Move the mallet to a suitable height, knock out one piece, watch the upper stack settle and lift the mallet back, experiencing the most immediately visible moment of this wooden game.
scene.paper-pinwheel.narrative.b3a93ac9:
Paper pinwheels are handmade toys shared by children in many places: bent paper blades sit around a thin axle, turning when caught by the wind or a person's breath. A paper pinwheel held by Museums Victoria in Australia was made in 1988 during an activity at Melbourne's Children's Museum. Its four paper blades are fixed with a pin and small bead to a wooden chopstick handle, providing a specific record of children's craft in the late twentieth century.

The museum places it in a family of wind-powered toys alongside paper aeroplanes and kites. Readily available paper, wooden strips and old packaging can move once folded and assembled. The enjoyment comes from imagining, making and observing natural forces; the small object preserved in Melbourne records just such a childhood experience. Gently turn the two-coloured paper blades, lift the wooden handle and give them another short spin, watching the bent paper slowly settle around the centre.
scene.chinese-steelyard.narrative.2de16e:
A steelyard makes weighing a directly visible relationship of balance. The beam is suspended from a lifting point, an object is placed at one end and the counterweight on the other side is moved until the beam becomes level. It handles the weight of everyday objects. Markings, lifting points and counterweights together determine a reading, allowing weight to be compared and recorded.

A nineteenth-century Chinese steelyard in the Science Museum Group's collection in Britain includes a pan, counterweight and wooden case, with different lifting points for different weighing ranges. Several ranges share one beam, demonstrating the ingenuity and portability of this weighing tool. Here a wooden beam and metal counterweight are used, with a citrus fruit in the shallow pan. Move the weight to the right, lift the ring and gently lower it again, observing how weights find a balance at the two ends. After moving the counterweight to find balance, lift and put back the whole scale in one continuous motion, preserving the balance between beam and pan.
scene.garden-croquet.narrative.2159bc09:
Croquet is part of British garden and lawn leisure culture. Players strike balls with long-handled wooden mallets, guiding them through hoops while considering direction, force and the next landing point together. Rules were being organised in nineteenth-century Britain. In 1866, Walter Whitmore-Jones drew up croquet rules at Chastleton House in Oxfordshire, linking the house's lawn with the history of the game.

Formal competition and playing with friends and family in a garden do not work in exactly the same way. Garden croquet can adapt its hoop layout to the available space, allowing people of different experience levels to join in. Its enjoyment comes from taking turns, judging a route and spending time together. Here you experience a single passage through a hoop: draw the mallet back, gently strike the coloured ball and watch it pass through the white hoop and roll a little further across the grass.
scene.welsh-drop-spindle.narrative.33a13:
In Welsh textile displays and craft teaching, drop spinning helps people rediscover how fibre becomes yarn. A wooden shaft fitted with a weighted whorl twists wool or other fibres as it turns. The spindle can hang below the thread while more fibre is drawn out, after which the spun yarn is wound back onto the shaft. It is an ancient textile tool used widely, rather than being unique to Wales.

Tudor-period teaching materials from a Welsh heritage organisation introduce spinning in the context of clothing production and women's daily work. Today the National Wool Museum in Carmarthenshire still teaches wool preparation and drop spinning, keeping the tools and skills in use. Gently spin the wooden whorl, lower it slowly, then lift it and let it settle. In this brief rise and fall, observe the connection between shaft, whorl and bundle of thread.
scene.scottish-plunge-churn.narrative.33:
On Tiree in Scotland's Inner Hebrides, the upright plunge churn was once an important tool for processing dairy produce in farming households. Local historical records and residents' memories show that it remained in use until the mid-twentieth century. Wooden staves form the body, metal hoops bind the sides and a wooden rod passes through the lid to a dasher inside. Moving it up and down with a slight turn gradually brings the milk fat together into butter.

Actual churning requires sustained work, often undertaken by women and children in the household. The finished butter could be eaten or salted for storage, closely connecting it with the family's food planning for the year. Here only a brief part of the rod's movement within the churn is retained: press down, lift and turn back, then raise the wooden lid a little, watching the wood grain and the surface of the milk grow still again.
scene.irish-bodhran.narrative.80d0b79c:
The bodhrán is a frame drum commonly heard in Irish traditional music, with a skin stretched over a round wooden frame. Players may strike it with a hand or beater and vary the sound through pressure on the skin and the position of their strokes. Its familiar accompanying role today has not remained unchanged since ancient times. The Irish Traditional Music Archive notes that it was once a vessel with everyday uses, becoming more prominently a musical instrument later.

Use of the frame drum in Irish traditional music grew markedly, especially in the second half of the twentieth century, while playing techniques continued to change through musicians' practice. Different strokes and control of the skin give this apparently simple round drum a rich range of sounds in ensemble playing. Alternate gentle touches on the drumhead with the double-ended wooden beater. After the three guided strokes, you can continue tapping; when you want to close, select "Finish", then turn the drum frame upright, observing the relationship between the beater's rebound and the round frame.
scene.french-coffee-mill.narrative.c0162:
The French hand-cranked coffee mill brings the grinding that precedes a cup of coffee to the everyday tabletop. The upper hopper holds the beans, the crank drives the grinding mechanism and the grounds fall into a small drawer below. The wooden box, metal parts and removable container together serve this kitchen task, putting preparation of the drink into a person's own hands.

The manufacturer Peugeot traces its coffee mill production to 1840 and still presents this manufacturing history today through hand-cranked wooden box models. The wooden box offers a warm touch, the crank and mechanism handle rotation and grinding, and the small drawer makes the grounds easy to remove. Turn the handle half a revolution, continue for another half, then pull open the small wooden drawer, observing the different textures of whole beans and fine grounds.
scene.japanese-wagasa.narrative.1f9d058b:
Gifu wagasa are one branch of Japan's paper umbrella craft. Bamboo ribs and washi paper together form an umbrella that can open and close. The availability of bamboo, washi and oils for coating umbrellas in the Nagara River basin supported local production. During the Edo period, umbrella making was also work that local samurai undertook to supplement their livelihoods, gradually developing into a regional craft with finely divided tasks.

Making a wagasa requires preparing bamboo ribs and the parts connecting them, applying paper and adding surface finishes, with each process working together. The umbrellas can provide protection from rain or sun and also appear in dance and theatre. Structure and surface treatment vary with their use, so a paper surface alone does not mean that an umbrella can only be displayed. Push the wooden runner up along the shaft to open the bamboo ribs and paper canopy. You can turn the handle freely to inspect the umbrella, or move the runner straight to the lower stop to close it, observing how this pale paper umbrella opens and folds.
scene.spanish-castanets.narrative.2a1f69:
Castanets have left a distinctive sound in Spanish music and dance. Two hollow wooden shells are joined by a cord, producing short rhythmic sounds when brought together. Actual playing requires the fingers to control their opening, closing and force. Museums preserve wooden castanets by twentieth-century Spanish makers as well as painted versions for travellers. The same instrument can belong to the stage, everyday music-making and the world of souvenirs.

Different woods, shell shapes and playing methods create variations, and dancers and makers continue to adapt them. The surviving shells, hollows and cords show how craft serves sound, and how a simple form becomes a rhythmic partner to dance. Let the wooden shells on the left gently meet, then listen to the right side answer. You can then continue playing in rhythm. When you want to close, select "Finish", leaving a short passage of rhythm in their crisp clicks.
scene.japanese-shishi-odoshi.narrative.6:
A shishi-odoshi is a bamboo water device that makes a knocking sound in Japanese gardens. An inclined bamboo tube pivots around a support. As water gradually fills it, the weight makes it tip; once the water empties, the tube returns and its tail strikes a stone. Accumulating water, a changing centre of gravity and the contact between bamboo and stone form a repeatable action.

The Japanese garden dictionary of the Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties explains that such devices were originally used to scare away deer and wild boar that damaged crops, later becoming features in gardens. The sound retains the device's practical origins while giving the garden's water an intermittent rhythm, alternating the wait for water to collect with a sudden knock. Guide water into the bamboo, support the tube as it gently tips, then let its tail return to the stone. With assistance from your hand, observe one cycle of filling and returning to knock.
scene.german-jumping-jack.narrative.ce4d:
Hampelmann is the German name for a string-operated jointed puppet. It combines painted wooden pieces, moving joints and fine cords; pulling the lower cord sets the figure's limbs in motion. A puppet dating to around 1910 in the Museum of European Cultures in Berlin, Germany, is painted as a clown in a tall hat. Its head and limbs can move, and the collection description also records the operating cords attached to the limbs.

The ingenuity of such toys lies in the connections behind them: a single cord transfers a hand's movement to several wooden pieces, giving a still figure a jumping pose. That early museum example combines a painted clown with movable wood, preserving the appearance of an early-twentieth-century toy. Gently pull the wooden bead to stretch the puppet's arms and legs, then release it and watch them fall, enjoying the movement created by simple materials.
scene.finnish-kantele.narrative.be11c3b5:
The kantele is a family of plucked string instruments in Finnish music; the small five-string instrument is just one form. The Finnish Kantele Association explains that this family is connected with related instruments elsewhere in the Baltic region. Today it includes wooden instruments with few strings, concert instruments with many more, and electric forms, showing continually developing sounds and shapes.

A wooden resonating body and metal strings form a structure that players sound with their fingers. It has a place in children's music education as well as contemporary composition, improvisation and performances in different styles, so the tradition continues to be used and changed. From the small instrument beside a beginner to playing on stage, the experience of plucking strings is passed on in different settings. Gently pluck the long, middle and short strings, watching their vibrations settle. After the three guided plucks, you can continue playing. When you want to close, select "Finish", keeping a short musical response of your own.
scene.estonian-village-swing.narrative.5:
Village swings in Estonia are connected with spring gatherings and seasonal life. The Estonian Open Air Museum explains that Easter can also be called the "swing holiday" locally, with traditional spring swinging often beginning at this time. Young men in the village built swings in suitable places, and the young women who came to enjoy them brought ribbons, butter, eggs or other gifts to thank the builders.

The custom belongs to a festival that both commemorates Christ's resurrection and welcomes spring, making the swing part of festive social life. The museum's swing grounds today also host Midsummer Eve and other gatherings, continuing a shared public life around the swing. Before you, a small wooden platform hangs from a wooden frame. Gently push it forwards, follow its swing back and slowly bring it to rest, feeling a brief back-and-forth movement within a gathering scene.
scene.french-petanque.narrative.a5ea3514:
La Ciotat in Provence, France, connects the formation of pétanque with an adjustment made on a local boules ground. The city's tourism organisation recounts that the player Jules Hugues had difficulty taking a run-up because of rheumatism, so Ernest Pitiot adopted a way of playing with both feet kept inside a circle and a shorter throwing distance. The first official competition was held locally in 1910.

It grew from the setting of the longer-distance Provençal boules game while allowing someone with limited mobility to continue taking part. Players send balls from the circle, trying to land close to the small target, making distance and landing position the focus of attention. This local account shows how a game can change its rules and spread. First send out the wooden target, then let two metal balls land nearby. Watch their rolling gradually stop and experience a brief moment of throwing.
scene.english-hearth-bellows.narrative.5:
Hand bellows were once an everyday tool for tending a hearth. Leather between two wooden boards forms an expanding air chamber. Separating the handles draws air in, while pressing them together sends it through the nozzle, allowing a person to direct airflow towards the fire. The object brings together woodworking, leather joints and the need to warm a home.

A pair of wooden and leather bellows dating to around 1900 in the National Trust's collection survives among the Drewe family collections at Castle Drogo in Devon, England, providing a specific date for this kind of household implement. The preserved wooden boards and leather keep the manual work of tending a household fire visible. Here plain wooden handles, folded leather edges and a brass nozzle present this structure. Lift, press together and release the handles, watching the air chamber open with the movement.
scene.mexican-metate.narrative.3a3784b0:
The metate grinding stone and long stone roller called a metlapil are a familiar pair of utensils in the foodways of Mexico and Mesoamerica. Grain is spread over the supporting stone surface and the long roller is pushed back and forth with both hands, gradually reducing maize and other ingredients. The Dictionary of Mexican Spanish still defines metlapil as a stone cylinder used to grind maize and other grains on a metate, retaining the connection between object and food.

The Colonial Museum in Colombia explains that this utensil originated in Indigenous societies in Mexico and Mesoamerica and entered wider kitchen life through exchanges of food practices during the colonial period. Back-and-forth grinding turns ingredients into a state suitable for cooking, a concrete and sustained part of preparing meals. Push forwards and grind back over the shallow stone surface, then return the roller to the rear edge, watching coarse grains and pale traces of flour gradually spread.
scene.czech-wooden-ratchet.narrative.dae:
The Czech wooden ratchet řehtačka is connected with Easter sound customs. The Český Dub local museum explains that church bells fall silent from Maundy Thursday to Holy Saturday in remembrance of Christ's Passion. Folk accounts say that the bells "fly to Rome". During this time, ratchets and other sounds call people to worship, and these instruments later also became part of Easter festivities.

The museum's ratchets vary in size and shape, from familiar small pieces to larger cross-shaped objects, showing how festival sounds can be produced by different structures. The spring of the wood and the successive movements of the teeth turn a hand's rotation into sound. The plain wooden frame before you turns around its handle, with the teeth bending the wooden tongue one after another and letting it spring back. Slowly turn through one revolution and observe how wood produces a continuous rhythm.
scene.puerto-rican-guiro.narrative.79ced:
The güiro is a rhythmic instrument used in Puerto Rican and Caribbean music. A Puerto Rican example in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York is dated to the nineteenth century and made from gourd and wood, providing material evidence of local use of this kind of object. The surviving gourd, ridges and scraper show how natural materials become sound-producing objects in music.

A güiro often uses a hollow gourd with a row of ridges cut into its surface. As a wooden stick or comb-like scraper moves along them, the continuous friction makes the music's rhythm. Versions in wood, metal and other materials also exist, with more than one shape and sound. Here the meeting of gourd and wooden stick is retained: scrape down along the ridges and back again, then continue playing if you wish. When you want to close, select "Finish" to move the stick away, listening as the beat ends in its lingering sound.
scene.valencian-folding-fan.narrative.dc:
Aldaia, in Spain's Valencia region, is an important town for folding-fan making. Records compiled by its fan museum show that at least eighteen families were practising the craft in 1857. Workshops gradually developed in the second half of the nineteenth century, becoming part of local industry in the twentieth. A light folding fan connects several kinds of work, including woodworking, cutting, assembly and painted decoration.

The ribs support the fan leaf and determine how it opens and closes. Wood is combined with silk or other fabrics, requiring careful work to produce regular folds. Women's work in workshop production and decoration is also part of this local craft history. Slowly open the fan, wave it gently once, then close it to a half-open position, observing how the wooden ribs gather around a single pivot.
scene.mexican-tortilla-press.narrative.2:
In Mexican tortilla making, a manual press flattens a round ball of masa dough into a thin disc ready for the next stage of cooking on a griddle. Upper and lower plates work with a long handle, while two thin liners help separate the dough from the plates. Wooden, cast-iron, aluminium and steel presses are all used. Their weight, dimensions and pressure also affect the thickness of the uncooked tortilla.

This kitchen tool has not remained in the past simply because it is operated by hand. Contemporary producers who make and sell Oaxaca-style presses still discuss even pressure, how to peel back the liners and the needs of different tortilla sizes. The meaning of the object lies in the experience of preparing everyday food. Close the wooden plate, press down the long handle, then release it and open the lid. Watch the dough become an uncooked tortilla between the liners, experiencing a part of preparation before griddle cooking.
scene.ghanaian-oware.narrative.ea7e7fe1:
Oware is a name for a board game used by Akan-speaking communities in Ghana and is also common in Asante game-playing life. A typical board has two rows of six pits, beginning with forty-eight pieces divided among them. Players lift the pieces from a pit on their own side, sow them into successive pits and capture pieces from the opposite side according to the rules. This seemingly simple sowing requires attention to how quantities change across the board.

It can be a serious contest or an activity that gathers relatives, friends and onlookers together. Different forms have their own rules: Abapa, common in Ghana, differs from the Nam-nam played by children. A single move cannot explain an entire game. Here, from an opening position of four pieces in each pit, lift the contents of one pit and drop them one by one into neighbouring wooden pits, first getting to know the basic act of "sowing seeds".
scene.chinese-rattle-drum.narrative.0075:
The sound of the rattle drum was once a signal used to attract customers in Chinese streets and lanes. An exhibition on peddler paintings at the National Palace Museum in Taipei explains that travelling sellers carried shoulder poles or pushed carts, shaking small drums and singing descriptions of their goods and uses to draw women and children. Southern Song painter Li Song of Qiantang depicted an old peddler shaking a drum with children gathering around him in Peddler and Children.

These images show the drum's relationship with urban and rural trade, everyday goods and children's lives, and demonstrate a recognisable setting for its use in the Southern Song. The painted drum calling customers also connects the peddler's work with children's anticipation. The small double-sided drum before you has two wooden beads attached by fine cords. Turn the handle right, turn back left and return it upright, observing how the beads alternately strike the drumskins. After the three guided actions you can continue. When you want to close, select "Finish" and let the drum slowly lower.
scene.chinese-tangram.narrative.4b190c99:
A tangram consists of seven geometric pieces that form a square and can be rearranged into many outlines: five triangles in different sizes, one square and one parallelogram. Known in China by names including qiqiao tu, its appeal comes from the continually changing relationships between a limited set of shapes.

Surviving pattern books, boxed puzzles and export records provide fairly clear evidence of its circulation in the early nineteenth century. A related pattern book published in 1813 and a puzzle craze in Europe and America around 1817–1818 show how it crossed regions through books and trade. Its pieces can form objects, animals and human poses, with simple outlines leaving room for observation and imagination. Four pieces are already in place. Move in the remaining three and watch the scattered outlines come together as a square.
scene.chinese-diabolo.narrative.6cc3159c:
The diabolo, or kongzhu, is a bamboo and wooden object in traditional Chinese games, with active traditions of making and playing in Beijing, Tianjin and elsewhere. An account in the Ming-period Dijing Jingwulüe and objects excavated from Dingling provide specific evidence for understanding its use at that time.

Diabolos come in forms including single and double wheels. Hollow discs are joined by a wooden axle. Holding sticks in both hands, the player pulls a string to accelerate the axle as it spins on the cord; wheels with whistle openings can also produce sound. Makers' knowledge of objects and players' throwing and catching skills together form this pastime. First lift the sticks to set the double wheels moving, then spread the string to toss and catch them gently. You can play a few more times; when you want to stop, lower the bamboo sticks and let the diabolo slowly settle on the string.
scene.korean-yutnori.narrative.14576000:
Yutnori is a board game often played by family and friends during the Korean New Year season. The National Folk Museum of Korea describes a festive period extending from Lunar New Year to the fifteenth day of the first lunar month. Each of four wooden sticks has a flat and a rounded side, and the combination after a throw determines a move of one to five spaces. Certain results allow another throw. Players take turns throwing and moving pieces, bringing together changes of chance and lively group discussion.

It was also once connected with agricultural hopes: there were beliefs that the winning side would enjoy a good harvest. Such beliefs belong to a particular festive life and do not mean that every throw predicts an individual's fate. Gather the sticks, throw them and let a blue piece advance according to the result. You can continue throwing from your current position. When you want to stop, select "Finish playing", experiencing a short stretch of the game's back and forth.
scene.russian-matryoshka.narrative.dd9b4:
The large wooden figure of a Russian matryoshka separates at the waist to hold a smaller one inside. Different stories describe how it first came into being. What can be established is that matryoshka dolls appeared publicly at the Paris Exposition in 1900 and gradually became popular collectables and gifts. Their history belongs to woodworking and painting as well as modern handicraft production and the circulation of goods.
