Twentieth-century Soviet production gave different places distinctive painting styles, with works from Semyonov and other centres each having their own appearance. Makers later continued changing characters and subjects, so there is no single standard set of clothing and patterns on the rounded wooden bodies. Lift off the outer part, tuck the small doll into the hollow and gently close along the seam, appreciating the ingenuity of wooden forms that nest one inside another.
scene.japanese-koinobori.narrative.351b7:
Around Children's Day on May 5 each year in Japan, carp streamers can often be seen filling with wind outside homes. Introductions to the custom usually trace it to the Edo period. Drawing on the Chinese legend of a carp swimming upstream and rising to become a dragon, people expressed hopes that boys would grow strong and achieve success. The hollow fish shapes seem to swim in the air when they catch the wind, making wishes for growth a visible part of the spring landscape.

The colours, numbers and family meanings of carp streamers also change. Earlier displays mainly used black carp; later, different colours and sizes were added, gradually creating combinations representing a family. Large flags in gardens and small ones on balconies adapt to different living spaces. Unfold a cloth carp's tail, pull the rope to raise it and secure the end, then quietly watch the fabric sway in the wind, holding the wish of welcoming a child's growth.
scene.japanese-kendama.narrative.dd96fcf:
Kendama developed in Japan as a skill game that can be played casually or studied seriously and in competition. The wooden handle has a large and a small cup on its sides, another cup at the bottom and a spike at the top. A cord connects it to a wooden ball, which players catch in a cup or align by its hole with the spike. The coordination of hands, eyes and body creates many movements from these simple parts.

Japanese records of kendama appear at least as early as an educational report from 1876. The "sun-and-moon ball" introduced in 1919 was an important predecessor of the modern form, and the Japan Kendama Association, established in 1975, further developed rules and competitions. These milestones show its continual organisation and evolution. Here catching is condensed into three gentle catches on the large cup, small cup and spike. The catches automatically coordinate with the movement, making the relationship between the ball's hole and the turning handle easier to see.
scene.indian-charkha.narrative.0bdd6249:
The charkha is a type of Indian hand-operated spinning wheel. A wooden wheel drives the spindle through a cord. The spinner turns the wheel with one hand and draws out fibres with the other, twisting loose cotton into thread; winding it on also requires stopping and adjusting the thread's position. Open wooden frames and versions that fold into a box reflect different needs in this everyday textile work.

In the early twentieth century, the spinning wheel also entered the public life of India's anti-colonial movement. Gandhi advocated local textile production and hand-spun khadi cloth, connecting spinning with resistance to British industrial textiles and the restoration of local production. It therefore has meaning both as a production tool and a symbol of social action, and cannot be understood simply as a decorative wooden wheel. Draw out the fibre, turn the wheel and return the thread to wind it on, condensing the coordination of actual spinning into a sequence that can be observed.
scene.german-nutcracker.narrative.be3774:
Seiffen, in Germany's Ore Mountains, is known for wooden toys and festive woodwork. As local mining declined, residents gradually turned to woodworking and turning for their livelihoods. Toy production increased by the mid-eighteenth century, later developing into household divisions of labour and export trade. Within this woodworking environment, the nutcracker acquired a distinctive human form, turning a tool for cracking nuts into a dressed, hatted and bearded wooden figure.

A Seiffen nutcracker dating to around 1957 in the Leipzig Museum of City History retains an operating lever on its back. The lever moves the lower jaw: the open mouth holds a nut and applies pressure as it closes. It also belongs to the world of Christmas wooden decorations, combining practical use and display. Lift the lever to open the mouth, put in the walnut, then press the lever to crack it, observing the linkage between the figure's back and lower jaw.
scene.mexican-molinillo.narrative.866870:
A molinillo is a wooden tool used in Mexican kitchens to whisk chocolate drinks. Its slender handle is rolled back and forth between the palms, moving the head's grooves and loose wooden rings to introduce air into the drink. The size, number of rings and carved grooves vary between tools. Beneath the rich variety of wooden forms lies the practical use of stirring drinks and producing foam.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds a late-nineteenth-century Mexican wooden molinillo, preserving a datable example of this everyday implement. Research today continues to explain its ingenuity: rotating the head near the liquid's surface makes it easier to introduce air, while stirring methods vary with users' experience. Place the head at the surface of the cocoa and roll the wooden handle left and right, watching the loose rings turn and fine bubbles collect.
scene.malawi-sansi.narrative.681164c8:
Among Chewa communities in central and southern Malawi and related communities speaking Chinyanja and other languages, the sansi is an instrument played by plucking metal lamellae with the fingers. The metal "tongues" are fixed to a wooden board, often with a wooden or gourd resonator. Makers may also use old spoon handles, bicycle spokes or spring wire, hammering the material into the required shapes and lengths.

A record by the Malawi National Commission for UNESCO explains that the shorter the vibrating part of a tongue, the higher its pitch. Alternating or simultaneous plucks with both thumbs can layer rhythm and harmony. Sansi music often adds subtle variations to repeated themes, creating melodies that cycle without being exactly the same. Here a simplified nine-key wooden board instrument lets you repeatedly tap or gently pluck any metal tongue, try forming a sound of your own and finish manually when you wish.
scene.chinese-suanpan.narrative.23780624:
Chinese zhusuan uses an abacus, representing numbers and performing calculations through the positions of its beads. It is connected with commercial calculation and education. The growth of the commodity economy during the Ming dynasty made zhusuan more widespread, while mathematical books such as Cheng Dawei's Zhizhi Suanfa Tongzong organised and disseminated the relevant knowledge. This calculation culture later also influenced Japan, the Korean peninsula and Southeast Asia.

Abacus beads are more than decoration. Upper and lower beads on the same rod have different values, while place values increase on successive rods to the left. Here the structure has two upper and five lower beads: an upper bead moved towards the beam counts as five, a lower bead as one, and the next rod to the left has ten times the value. Set three, eight and eighteen in turn, observing how units connect with tens and how finger movements turn abstract numbers into visible combinations.
scene.mongolian-felt-ger.narrative.8164a:
The portable structure of a Mongolian ger brings together woodworking, felt-making and sewing. Lattice walls fold together, roof poles rise to connect with a crown, felt and cloth cover the outside, and ropes and bands secure it all. Above all, it is a home that can be inhabited, taken apart, assembled and moved. How its materials work with everyday life says more about the craft than its round outline alone.

Records from Mongolia's cultural heritage organisation name places of transmission including Övörkhangai Province and Ulaanbaatar. Family members take part in making and assembly together, skilled craftspeople undertake the woodworking, and felt-making and sewing each require their own experience. Young people learn through apprenticeships and by observing their elders. Unfold the wooden lattice, lift the crown securely and place the white felt over the frame, condensing the many processes of making a home into three connections and observing how frame and covering support one another.
Peruvian mate burilado, the craft of engraving gourds, turns a dried gourd shell into a surface for storytelling. Important production areas include the Mantaro Valley in the Junín region and Huanta in the Ayacucho region. Engraving tools cut fine lines, joining scenes of farming, herding, festivals and village life across the curved surface. The objects thus preserve everyday scenes familiar to their makers.

In a 2014 interview with the Alfaro Núñez family of Cochas Grandes, Peru's Ministry of Culture recorded experiences of learning between brothers and making together with parents, children, nephews and nieces. Each person's engraving and colouring methods differ. The craft continues through family teaching and reaches wider places through the sale of works. Use the engraving tool to add leaves and hills, then gently wipe the surface, watching a group of simplified lines emerge on the warm-coloured gourd shell.
scene.venetian-glass-bead.narrative.3c52:
Glass bead production in Venice, Italy, can be traced to at least the fourteenth century, and Murano's glass industry is also closely connected with beadwork. Tiny beads are used for decoration, embroidery and assembly and were also trade goods exported to Africa, the Americas and India. In the nineteenth century, bead-making remained active while other glass production faced difficulties, leaving many richly coloured samples.

Different techniques produce different bead shapes. Small beads may be cut from hollow glass tubes, while lampworked beads are made by heating glass in a flame and winding it around a constantly turning metal wire. Beyond making the beads, the work of Venetian women who strung them also became part of memories of life in the streets and lanes. Turn the mandrel, wind on a coloured pattern and thread the bead onto a fine cord once the colour has set, looking closely at its translucent body.
scene.korean-bojagi-wrap.narrative.7f35c:
Bojagi are square Korean cloths used to wrap objects. They were part of daily life across social classes, used to transport and store things, cover food, protect objects and present gifts with care. Materials such as silk, ramie and cotton vary according to use. Many surviving wrapping cloths date from the Joseon dynasty, allowing us to see how fabric forms colour and composition beyond practical use.

The Los Angeles County Museum of Art's introduction gives particular attention to women's making and transmission of the craft. A wrapping cloth may also be a treasured household object passed to a daughter or daughter-in-law. In contemporary Korean gift-giving, wrapping a gift in cloth also carries the intention of sending good luck to its recipient. Gather the corners around the gift box, secure the ties and leave a message for the recipient, expressing care through a simple act of wrapping.
scene.vietnamese-bamboo-dragonfly.narrat:
Thạch Xá, at the foot of Tây Phương Mountain in Hanoi, Vietnam, developed a local craft around bamboo dragonflies that can "stand". A local tourism account places its emergence in the 1990s, when some woodworkers made small bamboo toys that later attracted visitors and traders, gradually becoming a village product and tourist souvenir. Thạch Xá today belongs to the Tây Phương area, and the craft continues in local workshops.

Makers choose mature bamboo, carve the body, long wings and slender tail, carefully adjust weight and balance, and finish by painting it by hand. A tiny supporting point can hold the outspread wings through the coordination of material and form. Gently rest the pointed beak on the tip of the branch, then nudge a wing or the body to see how the bamboo dragonfly sways and slowly regains its balance.
scene.turkish-ebru-paper.narrative.a83b4:
Turkish ebru is a craft that transfers colours floating on a liquid surface onto paper. Craftspeople first prepare a liquid that can support the pigments, then use brushes and tools to scatter and draw out coloured patterns before letting paper receive the design. Flowing colours can form flowers and leaves, interlacing lines or stone-like patterns, and the work is closely connected with bookbinding and paper decoration.

The craft is taught between masters and apprentices through explanation, observation and repeated practice. Judging pigments, the liquid surface and timing requires long experience. Today's workshops also bring different people together to learn, continuing an observation of colour and movement on sheet after sheet. Comb out the coloured pattern, let the paper gently touch the water's surface and slowly lift its edge, watching a brief flow remain on the paper.
scene.indonesian-angklung.narrative.6ad6:
The angklung is closely connected with bamboo music traditions in West Java and Banten, Indonesia, with relevant records dating to at least the early eighteenth century. Several bamboo tubes are suspended by rattan in a bamboo frame and produce sound when shaken or struck. One instrument usually supplies one note or one chord; many people's sounds must join to make a complete melody, so ensemble playing depends particularly on listening and cooperation.

It has taken part in community activities such as rice planting and harvesting, while new forms of performance continue to emerge. In 1938, Daeng Soetigna developed an angklung using Western scales, creating more possibilities for repertoire and teaching. Schools and communities became important places of transmission. Hold the bamboo frame or tubes and shake them freely back and forth as often as you like, letting the bamboo sound follow your hand's rhythm. When you want to close, gently select "Finish experience".
scene.weifang-paper-kite.narrative.9938a:
The kites of Weifang in Shandong, China, connect bamboo and wooden craft, painting on paper and the experience of flight. National intangible cultural heritage materials trace kite-making in Yangjiabu to the Ming dynasty and record that kites had become an important local handicraft during the Qianlong reign of the Qing dynasty. Later developments included flat, rigid-wing, soft-wing and string forms, allowing kites to be viewed on the ground and take different postures in the wind.

Making one requires attention to the bending of bamboo strips, symmetry between the sides and the placement of the bridle. Bright colours make its form easier to recognise in the sky. The craft continues within families and between masters and apprentices, passing on both judgement of materials and experience of flying. Close the paper wings of the swallow-shaped kite into place, pull the line taut and let it rise into the wind, observing how thin paper spreads across its bamboo frame.
scene.chinese-shadow-puppet.narrative.50:
Chinese shadow puppetry uses figures cut from animal hide or cardboard to perform stories with light and a translucent screen. The figures' parts are connected and moved by rods such as bamboo sticks. Performance also involves singing, music and oral and practical teaching between artists. Song-dynasty texts and related images already show fairly developed shadow performances, preserving an early appearance of this art.

Regional shadow traditions are not all the same. Haining in Zhejiang has its own singing styles and dialect and has also appeared at local occasions including weddings, birthday celebrations and prayers to deities. Other regions have their own repertoires and performance practices. Here you view a coloured paper bird from behind the screen. Lift the main rod, then move the wing rod, letting the joints and the shadow on the screen spread their wings together. Observe how manipulation behind the screen becomes movement in front of it.
scene.faroese-wool-knit.narrative.9ef67b:
In the Faroe Islands of the North Atlantic, wool is closely connected with everyday clothing and household work. The Faroes' official cultural portal introduces its value through the local saying "wool is gold". Prepared and spun wool becomes knitted clothing and continues to be used in contemporary design and the clothing industry.

Knitting knowledge lives beyond display cases. Official accounts record everyday knitting at home, at school and while travelling, and describe knitting circles in which women meet regularly to talk and continue the craft. Yarn passes continually through hands in these everyday gatherings, and experience of making clothing is passed on through conversation and demonstration. Guide the wooden needle into an old loop and bring out a new one, then look at the cream-white and grey fabric, getting to know how one stitch joins the knitting already there.
scene.niue-shell-necklace.narrative.8715:
Niue's kahoa hihi yellow shell necklaces use the small yellow shells of land snails found in coastal scrub on the island. Makers clean and pierce the shells, then string them into necklaces. A feature by the Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa traces early written records to the beginning of the twentieth century and describes how the adornment continues to be used in dance costume and gift-giving.

Gifts on the island may be offered to visiting guests, while overseas Niuean communities also use the necklaces to retain a connection with home. Shell colour, gathering materials and making experience turn them into memories of home that can be worn or given to others, reaching more distant places as people travel. Thread the final prepared yellow shell onto the fine cord, then draw the ends together so the small shells form an arc, looking closely at the warm yellow of this local craft.
scene.polish-paper-cut.narrative.bd2e647:
Polish folk paper-cutting is called wycinanki. In the first half of the nineteenth century, rural households began decorating windows with openwork paper ornaments, later pasting coloured designs on walls, stoves and beams to refresh rooms before festivals. Cutting along the edges of folded paper produces symmetrical flowers, leaves and animals; layering papers of different colours creates rich, vivid decoration.

Regional crafts differ. Single-colour tree-shaped cut-outs are common in the Kurpie Green Forest region, while Łowicz is known for layered coloured paper and scenes of human life. Making and teaching within households bring an ordinary sheet of paper into memories of local life. Here a small flowering branch remains: cut the last paper edge and slowly unfold it, observing how the two sides previously folded together meet.
scene.uzbek-clay-bowl.narrative.1fce4020:
Uzbek pottery is connected with everyday vessels for serving food and storing things. Bowls, plates, pots and bottles bring clay into household life. By the nineteenth century, areas including Fergana, Bukhara–Samarkand and Khorezm had developed distinctive pottery schools. Production centres such as Rishtan, Gijduvan and Khiva each accumulated their own experience of vessel forms, colours and decoration.

Pottery passes through selecting clay, forming, drying and firing, with different approaches for glazed and unglazed wares. During throwing, the wheel turns wet clay and the pull of the hands gradually forms its walls. Painting patterns and adding glaze belong to other, later tasks. Turn the wooden wheel and slowly draw upwards along the wet clay, letting a small bowl take shape. The experience ends with a clay body that is still wet and unfired.
Chinese woodblock printing carves text or images in reverse into a wooden block, transferring them to paper through inking, laying on paper and rubbing. Surviving prints and documentary evidence date to the Tang dynasty. From the Song dynasty onwards, woodblocks continued to be used to make books and did not immediately disappear with the arrival of movable type. Wooden blocks, paper, ink and the experience of carvers and printers together supported the spread of knowledge.

Yangzhou is one important place of transmission for this craft. Qing-dynasty book carving and modern workshops and printing organisations preserve a path of continued making and teaching. The palm-fibre brush used to apply colour and the palm-fibre pad used to press and rub the paper have different purposes. Gently pass the rubbing pad over the back of the paper, then lift a corner to see the inked branches and leaves transferred from the block, learning about this small part of the printing process.
scene.czech-bead-star.narrative.6facb259:
Around Poniklá in northern Bohemia, Czechia, hollow glass beads are made into Christmas tree ornaments. A craft introduction from the Czech Embassy in Estonia records that the fashion for decorating Christmas trees encouraged local bead ornament production in the late nineteenth century. Stars, angels and all kinds of miniature everyday objects became shapes that could be hung.

Behind one lightweight ornament are different tasks including working glass, cutting, colouring and assembly. Families and workshops pass down this experience. Poniklá's Rautis production tradition continues today, also introducing visitors to the assembly process. Here a silver and blue six-pointed star is used. After attaching the final string of beads, you can turn it freely to see the front and back and watch the bead surfaces catch the light. When you have seen enough, tap to pause and enjoy its sheen.
scene.fijian-woven-fan.narrative.6e04d39:
Pandanus leaves in Fiji are used for everyday goods including fans, mats and clothing. A nineteenth-century Fijian woven fan preserved by the Torquay Museum provides a dated example of this material knowledge. The fan's meaning comes first from daily use and its maker's understanding of leaves, supports and connections.

An iri fan in Auckland Museum records a structure in which leaf strips are wound around a reed framework, a split wooden handle grips the fan leaf, and leaf strips bind it securely. From edge to handle, the connections between materials determine both shape and how it is held and used. Secure the binding at the upper end of the wooden handle, then place the leaf fan on its display stand, looking closely at how strips, framework and handle support one another.
scene.amazigh-woven-rug.narrative.89bea4:
The colours of Moroccan Amazigh textiles connect with mountain households' knowledge of wool processing and dyeing. Research by the Dar Si Said Museum of Weaving and Carpets in Marrakesh records mothers teaching daughters about materials and dyes. Different areas of the Atlas Mountains use dyestuffs including madder and pomegranate peel, producing distinctive reds, yellows and oranges.

This tradition also changes. The research records the gradual introduction of synthetic dyes from the late nineteenth century, while twentieth-century rugs from the Haouz region in the collection provide visible material examples. The stripes and geometric blocks here are an independent colour arrangement for a small woven rug. Finish the last row with the wooden shuttle, then move the rug to the display rack, observing how warp and weft join soft wool into a piece of fabric.
scene.slovak-wire-bird.narrative.fd05d8f:
Slovak wire craft, drotárstvo, was once connected with the repair work of travelling craftspeople and later also produced household goods, toys and decorative objects. Metal wire can be bent and wound together, forming light shapes from continuous lines. A technology of everyday livelihood thus gradually entered new areas of creation, appearing in today's exhibitions both as useful objects and as art.

Craft exhibition materials from Žilina record wire sculptures from the 1940s and more explorations in wire art after the 1960s. Materials, joining methods and forms vary between makers; a bird is simply one available subject. Attach the wing, then place the bird on its wooden perch, observing the outline formed by fine wire and the light entering the spaces between its contours.
scene.hungarian-embroidery-hoop.narrativ:
Hungarian folk embroidery has many local styles, varying in colour, stitches and the density of patterns. No single flower can represent the whole country. Embroidery appears on linen, hemp and cotton as well as leather and woollen goods. Needle and thread decorate clothing and household textiles, connecting material, purpose and local aesthetics.

The Hungarian Heritage House records that village embroidery was once part of household craft and that by the early twentieth century some embroiderers also sold their work at markets. This change allowed it to continue in everyday life while also entering craft teaching and exchange. Here a simple flower of thread introduces the relationship between coloured yarn and cloth. Use the spool to add the flower to the stretched fabric, then place the wooden hoop on its display support, looking closely at the petal colours and stitches.
The Triana district of Seville, Spain, has a distinctive local memory of pottery workshops and decorative tile production. Today's Triana Ceramics Centre occupies the former Santa Ana factory, preserving late-nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century kilns, clay storage basins, mineral-grinding facilities, pigment containers and tables used for painting tiles.

These remains show that the glaze colours on a wall come from a whole body of work: processing clay, preparing colours, painting and firing. The factory also made tiles used by architect Aníbal González in the Plaza de España, connecting workshop craft with the city's architecture. The fired blue and white tiles before you are missing a central piece. Fill the space, then place the whole wooden frame on the display support and appreciate the patterns that meet across its joints.
scene.sicilian-painted-cart.narrative.a2:
The Sicilian carretto in Italy was once a wooden cart used for rural transport and agricultural work. The painted cart museum in Aci Sant'Antonio places its flourishing within road life in the first half of the nineteenth century. As carts travelled with their loads, they also brought the skills of carpenters, carvers and painters into everyday life. Surviving painted carts later became important objects for viewing local history and craft.

Their decoration goes beyond bright colour. Wheels may be finely carved, and panels on the body tell stories of historical, epic or religious figures, giving a practical object images that can be read. The small cart before you retains the enjoyment of painted woodwork through simple colour blocks. Fit the wooden wheel, move the cart onto the display mat and look closely at the colours of its spokes and body.
scene.bai-indigo-cloth.narrative.3acdac8:
Zhoucheng in Dali, Yunnan, China, is an important place of transmission for Bai tie-dye. Local surveys record household tie-dye workshops operating during the Republican period. Making, trading and teaching within village families turn blue and white patterned cloth into both an everyday item and a bearer of experience with dyes, needles and thread.

Tie-dye begins by stitching, binding, knotting or otherwise tightening parts of the cloth so that dye cannot easily enter. Repeated dipping, unpicking and rinsing reveal undyed patterns against a blue ground. The cloth appears in clothing, tablecloths, door curtains and other daily goods, while the craft is passed on within families and workshops. Here you begin with cloth that has already been tied and dyed. Lower it into clean water, watch it unfold and drape it over a wooden pole to dry, noticing the soft, never quite identical variations along the blue and white edges.
scene.ndebele-painted-house.narrative.55:
Ndebele house painting in South Africa creates striking walls through clear geometric boundaries and vivid colours. It is closely connected with women's painting experience in families and communities. Artist Esther Mahlangu recalls learning from her mother and grandmother as a child, practising first behind the house and painting at the front only after receiving approval. A home's wall can thus be a place both to learn and to display skill.

Iziko Museums' account of her retrospective identifies a 1989 exhibition in Paris as an important moment in her international recognition. She subsequently brought this visual language to canvas and other surfaces. Her personal experience shows how skills from the home can gain new spaces for display and continue developing. Fit a small coloured panel into the blank area of the model house's wall, then move it onto the platform and quietly observe a simplified geometric colour arrangement.
scene.purepecha-copper-bowl.narrative.81:
Santa Clara del Cobre is in Michoacán, Mexico, where local copperworking history can be traced through archaeological remains and colonial production records. Copper was worked in the area before the Spanish arrived, and a royal smelting facility existed in the early seventeenth century. Today copper remains an important material in the town's workshops, exhibitions, sales and memories of local craft, with skills continually changing under different historical conditions.

Local hammered copper objects include pots, plates and fruit containers, as well as decorative works for appreciation. Fine hammer marks and rolled rims draw attention to the shapes formed by working metal. Here you begin by caring for a copper bowl. Gently wipe it with a soft cloth, then place it on soft felt, looking closely at the copper colour as it slowly changes with the light.
scene.welsh-love-spoon.narrative.bc0b01b:
A Welsh lovespoon is a finely carved wooden gift used to express affection. Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales preserves an example inscribed with the date 1667, and many intricate examples survive from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Its exact origins remain a subject of discussion, but the practice of a suitor carving a spoon and giving time and skill to a beloved has become an important memory of this craft.

Lovespoons are often carved from a single piece of wood, with hearts, chains or other openwork designs on the handle. Different makers and givers may give their works meanings of their own. Today they are also used for commemorative occasions including weddings, birthdays, anniversaries and christenings. Gently wipe the bowl of the spoon, then hold the handle and place it on the display support, looking closely at grain and carving and pausing with a gift of affection ready to be given.
scene.barcelos-clay-rooster.narrative.7b:
Pottery and clay figures in Barcelos, northern Portugal, have long been part of local households' livelihoods and market life. Known in Portuguese as figurado, the figures are formed by hand, in moulds or through both methods together. Makers depict people, animals and everyday scenes, and their works were sold through markets, festivals and pilgrimage gatherings.

In the mid-twentieth century, works by makers such as Rosa Ramalho gained wider attention. Clay figures previously associated with toys and markets gradually became distinctive images of local culture, and the rooster became a widely recognised emblem of Barcelos. From form to colour, makers have their own expression, giving the same rooster outline different appearances. Pick up the brush and finish the pattern on its chest, then place the clay rooster on the round platform and appreciate its clay, colours and handmade form.
scene.finnish-birch-basket.narrative.14e:
Woven birch-bark containers in eastern Finland were once part of everyday sowing and storage. The National Museum of Finland explains that a birch-bark container called a kylvinkopsa could hold flour, grain and salt. In agricultural life, the material and shape of a container had to meet the needs of carrying, accessing and preserving food.

The museum also distinguishes eastern woven birch-bark vessels from western containers made of bent aspen boards, showing how different regions used different materials to meet similar needs. The article records that hand sowing continued until seed drills gradually became widespread in the 1920s and 1930s, a history that also shows how objects change with methods of production. Attach a curved handle to the woven birch basket and set it on the cloth mat. Look at the interlaced strips and grains inside, appreciating details of everyday craft.
scene.croatian-licitar-heart.narrative.1:
The decorated licitar biscuits of northern Croatia come from a continuing local gingerbread craft. Cultural authorities introduce it within the background of gingerbread-making spreading through medieval European monasteries. After reaching the region, it continued through craftspeople's production and teaching. Makers in the past also dealt in honey and candles, connecting the craft closely with household livelihoods.

Dough is shaped, baked, dried and decorated before becoming a work that can be given. Hearts are especially common, decorated with icing lines, small mirrors, names and dates as wedding mementos or expressions of affection. Particular designs are chosen by makers and givers. The red heart before you is already shaped. Add icing with the piping bag, then hang its fabric ribbon on the wooden peg, leaving a colourful expression of care for someone important to you.
scene.catalan-festival-giant.narrative.6:
In Catalonia, Spain, gegants, or giant figures, take part in local festivals with music and dance. They often have locally familiar names and appearances, and making, maintaining and taking them out requires teamwork. Associations of giants still carry out preservation, research and teaching activities in music, dance and related skills.

Different towns have histories of their own. Catalan heritage records document giants in L'Arboç in 1770, a named local pair in 1827 and replicas made for use in events in 1984. The succession of old and new giants keeps locally familiar figures present at festivals. Pin a floral badge onto the small model giant, then place it on the round platform. Examine its clothing and form and imagine the preparations behind a street procession.
scene.sorbian-painted-egg.narrative.ebb1:
In Sorbian communities in Lusatia, Germany, Easter eggs are both a detailed craft and part of gift-giving between relatives and friends. The Sorbian cultural information centre records that in some families around Muskau and in central Lusatia, godparents give children festive gifts that include decorated eggs. The growth and vitality associated with the egg are entrusted as good wishes for the recipient.

There are different techniques for decorating eggs: wax can leave dots, short lines and triangles before successive dye baths, or a dyed shell can be scratched. Today's egg markets in Bautzen and Drebkau still let people watch artists closely and try decorating eggs. Use the brush to add a flowering pattern to the blue-green shell, then place it in the ceramic cup, leaving colour for a festive gift.
scene.basque-sunflower.narrative.a342398:
At the Orozko Ethnographic Museum in Spain's Basque region, the eguzkilore thistle is introduced within the lives of mountain herders and farming households. Its name means "flower of the sun", and the local practice of placing it at a house door can still be seen. The doorway is both an everyday entrance and exit and, in folk imagination, a household boundary in need of protection.

The beliefs recorded by the museum connect eguzkilore with protection against evil spirits, witchcraft, illness and thunderstorms. The flower by the door joins observation of a natural form with a wish to protect the family, and remains a recognisable local cultural image. Here the floral ornament is made from paper and wood. Fit its centre and hang it on the doorway's wooden peg, letting the radiating outline of eguzkilore become a welcoming wish.
scene.breton-banner.narrative.48aa134c:
A Breton pardon in France is a Catholic pilgrimage and festival centred on a local patron saint. France's Ministry of Culture connects the development of these events with fourteenth-century popular devotion and ideas of the forgiveness of sins. They later became interwoven with gatherings, song, dance and other community life, forming many festivals with distinct local features.

Besides Mass, participants process behind banners, crosses or sacred images, and some processions go to holy springs. Parishioners and volunteers prepare and maintain the events together. Banners in the procession make a local community's reverence and gathering visible in the streets. The small banner here uses wave and sun patterns. Fasten its cloth loops on the crossbar, then place its pole in the display base, experiencing the process of preparing a banner.
Lithuanian sodai literally means "gardens", but these are structures of straw suspended in the air. Fine threads pass through hollow stalks, connecting diamonds and pyramids joined above and below. The tradition is passed on across the country and has survived especially long in Aukštaitija. People associate its clear geometric order with life, fertility, harmony and the order of the world.

Straw gardens were hung above cradles to hold hopes for newborns and also appeared above wedding tables and in family spaces on Christmas Eve or at Easter, expressing good wishes for newlyweds and relatives. Today they continue to be used for weddings, interior decoration and craft teaching, holding both family memory and contemporary aesthetics. Attach the small lower diamond, then hang the whole straw garden on the workshop's wooden frame, quietly observing the light-filled spaces joined by straw and thread.
scene.dalarna-wooden-horse.narrative.f30:
The wooden horse of Dalarna, Sweden, has brought local carving and painting into a wider world. The Dalarna Museum gives particular attention to the 1939 New York World's Fair, where a large red wooden horse in front of the Swedish pavilion attracted attention. A local souvenir thus became more widely established as a cultural emblem of Sweden. A regional wooden horse entered an international exhibition and more people's image of Sweden.

The museum holds many horses, from early examples to contemporary free interpretations, reminding us that colour, posture and decoration have always varied. Behind the familiar outline are different craftspeople's ways with wood and brush; local craft continues developing through these small differences. Wipe the painted saddle with a soft cloth, then place the wooden horse on its base, looking closely at the details where wooden body and painted surface meet.
scene.aland-votive-ship.narrative.aff06c:
Church ship models in Finland's Åland Islands bring local maritime life into churches. Saint Andrew's Church in Lumparland preserves a model made in 1836, which parish records say was donated the following year by the merchant Carl-Gustav Löthman. Such objects give identifiable dates to the connections between donors, ships and churches.

Saint Anne's Church in Kökar also holds a wooden ship model, linked in local accounts to a resident's encounter with a pirate ship in 1733. The different histories of donation and local stories make churches places that preserve maritime memory. This small scene begins with those memories: raise the mast and place the ship model on its cradle, with the option to leave a message of gratitude of your own.
scene.blang-tea.narrative.2ad10a36:
The ancient tea forests of Jingmai Mountain in Pu'er, Yunnan, China, are jointly maintained by Blang, Dai and other communities. UNESCO's heritage description traces the local practice of growing tea beneath the forest canopy to the tenth century. Tea trees grow alongside tall forest trees, linking villages, tea plantations and forests in a cultivation system adapted to the mountain environment and monsoon climate.

Social relationships also sustain the tea mountain. Local communities' land management, festivals and beliefs in tea ancestors and nature spirits take part in caring for and continuing the tea forests, allowing cultivation and local memory to endure together. Before you is an everyday tea break: add leaves to the pot, pour a cup and quietly observe the tea's colour. Look back from the cup towards the tea mountain and remember the people who have long cared for these woods.
scene.minangkabau-spinning-top.narrative:
This tabletop wooden top is a small toy designed for a brief pause. Its rounded body, wooden cap at the axle's end and wrapped cotton cord are connected, while a pale circle on the board provides a position for pulling the cord. Pull the wooden bead at the cord's end and the winding gradually loosens, setting the top spinning in place. Then gently touch the cap and watch it slowly settle; the wood grain and coloured rings before and after the spin become easier to distinguish.

This contemporary tabletop play focuses on the hand's actions and the object's response. You complete the rhythm of starting and stopping before you. It can simply be a game or a moment of stepping away from busyness. Finally, quietly observe the wooden top and loosened cord. If you want to record how it felt, leave a message of your own.
scene.chinese-incense.narrative.f6a5488e:
Mazu belief is closely connected with Putian and Meizhou Island in Fujian, China, and coastal communities. Devotees revere Mazu as a deity who protects seafarers and brings safety, while temples and worship spread overseas with migration. Among the earlier surviving records is the 1150 inscription on the rebuilding of the Shunji Temple at the ancestral temple of Shengdun, allowing us to trace the development of this faith through Song-dynasty writing.

Offering incense is part of specific religious practice. A field study of Chinese Mazu temples in Thailand records incense offerings, other offerings and prayers for safety, also showing how different communities incorporate local languages and customs. Here you experience only a brief part of arranging the incense objects: move aside the censer lid, place a slender stick of incense inside and quietly watch a line of smoke rise, learning about the reverence and prayers for peace connected with this act.
scene.hongsheng-red-string.narrative.d77:
A red cord unwinds from a spool, follows the circular groove in a wooden frame and is joined into a loop by a small clasp at its end. The craft before you centres on these simple objects. Follow the pale dots to wind the cord, bring the clasp to its fastening point and see how a loose strand becomes a complete circle. Red cord and pale wooden support complement each other, with attention on line, connection and the process of gathering it together by hand.

"Red Cord, Care for Yourself" places an intention of self-care within this contemporary craft. A circle of red cord moves from loose to connected, giving that intention a visible form. You can use it to remember a decision to treat yourself kindly or simply appreciate the loop. Leaving a message is your choice. It expresses your personal feelings now, without needing a fixed explanation.
scene.italian-ex-voto.narrative.34115bc5:
Near Deruta in Casalina, Italy, a Marian sanctuary is known for its ceramic votive plaques of thanksgiving. Local devotion to the Madonna dei Bagni took shape in the mid-seventeenth century, and construction of the sanctuary began in 1657. Devotees commissioned Deruta potters to depict experiences of receiving grace amid danger, illness or accidents on glazed ceramic plaques, leaving their thanks to the Virgin Mary on the sanctuary walls.

Hundreds of plaques spanning more than three centuries also preserve ordinary lives: homes, roads, work and sudden dangers all become stories within the pictures. Above all, they are offerings and acts of thanksgiving by Catholic devotees, while everyday scenes give concrete form to this faith. Here, drawing on the idea of recording thanks in an image, paint a homeward path and the light of a window, then leave a person or event you feel grateful for, placing gratitude within a small, simplified picture.
scene.czech-pilgrim-journal.narrative.e5:
A travel journal with a fabric bookmark lies on the table. Its pale pages show a mountain path, a stream and tree shadows, with a brass-coloured clip ready for the bookmark. Hold the corner of the cover and open it to the left, then place the fabric bookmark along the page edge. The small landscape that was hidden in the book is now fully revealed. Finally, gently touch the leaf-shaped marker to pause on this page.

This experience takes a pause on a contemporary journey as its subject. The mountain path on the page is an imagined landscape drawn for the scene. Turning the page suggests looking at the part already travelled, while placing the bookmark leaves a position for the next opening. These are personal associations the journal invites you to make. Even without travelling, you can use this page to recall a stretch of today's path, then continue at your own pace.
scene.omikuji.narrative.a2d47544:
Omikuji at Japanese shrines and temples are a practice of drawing lots to consult Shinto or Buddhist deities and read fortunes and admonitions. Kokugakuin University's explanation records earlier forms in which candidates' names were written on paper and lots were drawn to make religious decisions. More common today is shaking a cylinder containing numbered sticks and receiving a paper fortune with verses and predictions corresponding to the number drawn.

The cylinder and paper fortune thus carry the intention of consulting deities, and readers must also consider the verses and advice on the paper. Fortune texts and ways of handling them vary between shrines and temples. Besides asking about fortune, people may attend to reminders about conduct in the words. Here you follow the actions of shaking the cylinder, drawing a stick and unfolding the paper to read an original reminder written for everyday life, then put it into an envelope, leaving some thought for one small thing today.
scene.polish-blessing-basket.narrative.c:
In Polish Catholic families, Święconka is a custom of preparing food before Easter and bringing it to church for a blessing, usually on Holy Saturday. A small amount of festive food is placed in a basket lined with white linen or lace, which may also be decorated with green branches. Polish migrant families in Ireland still take part together in their parishes today. The size and contents of baskets vary between families, with the care of preparing food connected to Easter faith.

Parish blessing prayers associate bread with Christ as the "bread of life" and eggs with new life and the resurrection, remembering family and guests who share the food. A basket of everyday food thus also carries gratitude for life and reunion. Place bread and decorated eggs in the basket, pausing with a part of preparing it at home before going to church.
scene.navruz-sumalak.narrative.4cafc7e3:
In Uzbekistan, the spring celebrations of Navruz are often accompanied by a large pot of sumalak. Sprouted wheat is the main ingredient in this sweet food. Neighbours in a mahalla community divide the preparation work, take turns stirring around the pot and share the finished food with relatives, friends and neighbours. The long cooking gives people a chance to gather and makes food for welcoming the new season a result they can share.

Uzbekistan's official tourism organisation describes the current custom with particular attention to women taking turns tending the fire and pot, stirring through the night and sharing the food at the end. Spring renewal and generosity are expressed through this concrete work and cannot be reduced to a single wish by one person. Slowly stir the wooden spoon around the pot's edge, then serve a portion into a ceramic bowl and place it on the shared eating mat, experiencing a small part of cooking and sharing together.
scene.floating-lantern-loy-krathong.narr:
Thailand's Loi Krathong takes place on the full-moon night of the twelfth month of the Thai lunar calendar. People release krathong onto rivers, lakes, canals or the sea. The Tourism Authority of Thailand explains that these floats, decorated with flowers and candlelight, honour the water goddess and carry wishes to send away misfortune and welcome good luck. This meaning should be understood as the belief of participants.

Materials and activities vary by place. Cup-shaped banana-stem floats can be seen along the Mae Klong River in Samut Songkhram, for example, while other regions have forms such as linked strings of lights. The large Loi Krathong celebration in Sukhothai Historical Park has been held for decades, bringing ancient city remains, local legends and present-day gatherings into dialogue. Add flowers to the folded-leaf float, light the wick and gently push it onto the water. When releasing floats in real life, follow the material and clean-up requirements of the waterway you are visiting.
scene.omamori-cycle.narrative.efbdb25f:
Omamori are portable protective amulets offered by Japanese shrines and temples. A small talisman is often enclosed in brocade or another cloth pouch to be carried. People ask Shinto or Buddhist deities to protect matters such as safety, travel and health, while the pouch's appearance varies according to where it is received and the purpose of the prayer. Its placement and use differ from larger shrine talismans set in a household shrine or elsewhere at home.

Kokugakuin University's explanation of amulets records historical connections from the talisman-making practices of Onmyōdō and Buddhist temples to their later production by shrines as well. Ways of carrying them still differ today. The Association of Shinto Shrines explains that some people renew them at the year's end, while others carry them until the matter prayed for has been achieved. Choose a small pouch and attach its cord loop to a travel bag. On a return visit, you can also send it back to the wooden box with gratitude, experiencing the relationship between carrying and returning.
scene.shrine-suzu-bell.narrative.ba935ea:
Some Japanese shrines have a metal bell and a long rope in front of the worship hall. Visitors can ring it before paying respect to the deity. The Association of Shinto Shrines' public explanation connects the bell's sound with purification: sound accompanies reverence, allowing a person to approach the deity with composed intentions. This bell belongs to a space of worship and has a different use from wind chimes sounding beneath summer eaves.

Shrine visits often also include ritual washing, bows, clapping and prayer, with arrangements differing between shrines. Bell and rope give reverence an audible action, while the resonance remains in the space before the hall. Here you pause between pulling and listening: gently draw the thick rope downwards, release it and let it return, quietly listening as the sound gradually fades.
scene.st-brigids-cross.narrative.d69bf4d:
In Ireland, Saint Brigid's Day on February 1 is connected with hopes for spring in the agricultural year. On its eve, people weave crosses from rushes or straw and hang them in homes, cowsheds and stables, honouring Saint Brigid and praying for protection for family members and livestock. Their shapes are not uniform across the country; different regions preserve their own folding and weaving methods.

The now-familiar four-armed form spread more widely after it became a symbol of Irish television in the 1960s. Before then, diamond-shaped and other styles were also common. Such changes remind us that tradition continues to grow in family and public life. Guide four bundles of grass into the weaving points one by one, then hang the finished cross above the doorway, observing the texture left by interwoven stalks.
scene.bokjori.narrative.4f528553:
In Korean customs at the beginning of the year, bokjori are lucky bamboo strainers bought and hung for the New Year. Their form comes from a daily rice-washing utensil. People connect the act of scooping up grains with gathering good fortune, turning a kitchen object into an auspicious New Year item hung on an interior wall or elsewhere.

A folklore entry from the Academy of Korean Studies records that strainer sellers once called out along the streets from New Year's Eve through New Year morning, and some households wove them for sale during the quiet agricultural season. Jeolla, Gyeongsang and other regions also have different customs of buying and hanging them. Winter household craft, street trade at the start of the year and New Year decorations inside the home meet in this small bamboo implement. First try scooping a little rice to get to know its original purpose, then lift it by the bamboo handle and hang it, holding a wish for the new year.
scene.ema-votive-plaque.narrative.aac413:
Ema are offerings used in Japan for prayers and thanksgiving, found at shrines, temples and roadside places of worship. Kokugakuin University's Shinto materials explain their historical connection with offering horses and horse-shaped substitutes. Wooden ema excavated from Nara-period sites provide material evidence of early practice.

Later, ema no longer depicted only horses. From the Muromachi period onwards, subjects and sizes gradually diversified, including large votive works as well as the small hanging wooden plaques that continue today. People leave their wishes and gratitude on the wood, bringing different images together with personal experiences. Turn the plaque over to its back, where you may leave a short wish or leave it blank for now, then hang it beneath the crossbar. Looking back later, you can also leave an expression of thanks.
scene.clootie-well-rag.narrative.aeb309c:
At Munlochy in the Scottish Highlands, the clootie well connects water, trees and folk beliefs in healing. Its managing organisation explains that a cloot is a small piece of cloth: people dip it in the well water and tie it to a nearby branch, hoping that their illness or suffering will gradually diminish as the cloth decays. The cloth soaked in well water thus carries visitors' hopes for relief.

The scraps left on branches are traces of visitors' intentions and connect the care of the well site closely with this practice. Today the managers require small pieces of biodegradable pure cotton or pure wool to avoid environmental damage. Dip the cotton cloth, tie it to a low branch and release it to watch quietly. If you visit an actual holy well, follow its local care requirements.
scene.diya-oil-lamp.narrative.9ab66d79:
Oil lamps are visible objects in Hindu worship, with the meaning of their light understood in its particular setting. In describing its own practices, the Hindu Temple in Canton, Michigan, United States, explains that a priest moves a plate of small oil lamps clockwise before a sacred image. This offering of light is called Aarati, and devotees view the image by the light and pray.

The temple interprets light as knowledge. Related prayers concern moving from darkness to light and receiving right guidance, and its account also records beliefs in driving away unfavourable influences. In this community's worship, light, viewing the deity's image and silent prayer work together, connecting the light before a person with the guidance sought. Light three clay lamps in turn, let the front lamp move along an arc and gently return it to the plate, learning about the lamps and gestures used in an offering of light.
scene.votive-candle-catholic.narrative.3:
In Catholic churches, devotees light votive candles before images of Christ or saints, leaving intentions of petition and intercession in the light. Saint Patrick Parish in Tacoma, Washington, United States, connects candlelight with Christ as the "light of the world". The faithful honour Christ or the saint represented by the image and may ask saints to intercede with the Lord for themselves and others.

A burning candle offers a continuing visible presence: after a person returns to daily life, its flame still symbolises a willingness to remain before the Lord in prayer. This practice of lighting candles continues in parish life today, with each person bringing their own petitions. Place the candle in the holder, light its wick and leave a message for someone you miss, or quietly accompany this small light.
scene.daruma-eye-painting.narrative.8293:
Daruma making in Takasaki, Gunma Prefecture, Japan, is concentrated in the former Toyooka area. Takasaki City explains that the 1829 Takasaki Danzushō already records Daruma being sold at markets in text and images. After Yokohama's port opened in 1859, imported red pigment further encouraged production. The hariko method of layering paper over wooden moulds, drying it and removing the mould is an important part of local craft.

Takasaki Daruma connect crane-shaped eyebrows and tortoise-shaped beards with auspiciousness and longevity, and carry wishes for household peace, business prosperity or the achievement of a goal. The eyes are painted at two different times: first, with a wish in mind, paint the eye on the right as you face the Daruma. Once the wish has been fulfilled, or after a year has passed safely, paint the other eye. Here paint one eye, keep your wish and return the Daruma to the wooden base, letting the other eye's blank space accompany the path still unfinished.
scene.mizuhiki.narrative.adbeddcc:
Mizuhiki are decorative knots made of fine paper cord, used in Japan on monetary gift envelopes, celebratory envelopes and carefully prepared gifts. Cords made from washi can bend, cross and tighten into knots, letting the wrapping itself convey the giver's feelings. Nagano Prefecture's account connects the "knot" with relationships between people, explaining that its meaning lies in the exchange of gifts as well as decoration.

Iida in Nagano is an important production centre. The area developed paper cords called motoyui for tying hair during the Edo period. After hairstyles changed and demand fell in the Meiji period, the craft turned towards mizuhiki and gift-envelope decoration. This is a history of material skills adapting to changes in life. Form a loop around the paper envelope, pass through it and tighten the knot, then write a wish for the recipient, leaving the care of gift preparation in a simplified knot ornament.
scene.milagros.narrative.9e1b9324:
Milagros means "miracles" in Spanish. In Mexico and other parts of Latin America, it also refers to small metal charms offered to saints. Devotees pin them to crosses, sacred images or near altars to ask for help, healing and protection, or to give thanks after believing they have received grace. Shapes including body parts, people, animals and objects can connect with different personal experiences.

The Lam Museum of Anthropology's account places this practice in the encounter between Catholicism spread during the Spanish colonial period and local offering customs. It is not a dictionary of wishes that can be read mechanically by shape. The meaning of the same small charm may vary with its giver, and charms may also appear in contemporary art. Choose a charm and hang it on the wooden frame, then leave your own petition or thanks, retaining its background of expressing intentions to saints.
scene.phuang-malai.narrative.cdfbdd11:
Phuang malai are Thai garlands strung from fresh flowers, given to welcome guests, honour respected people and express thanks. Clusters of flowers are joined, with a ring and hanging ornaments that allow the sentiment to be held in the hands. In introducing Thailand's 2019 ASEAN chairmanship emblem, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs also used malai to express welcome and respect, showing that the garland remains a recognisable image in contemporary hospitality and courtesy.

For Mother's Day in Thailand, white jasmine has a particular family meaning, symbolising maternal love. Children thank mothers and the elders who care for them with flowers or garlands. Since August 12 was adopted as Mother's Day in 1976, this gratitude has had an annual occasion celebrated together. String the jasmine clusters one after another, secure the knot and place the garland on the small platform, leaving a message for someone you want to thank.
scene.woodfish.narrative.1886b116:
The wooden fish is a wooden percussion instrument used in East Asian Buddhist chanting. A wooden mallet strikes its hollow body to accompany the chant. The Metropolitan Museum of Art dates a wooden fish from Yunnan, China, to the early twentieth century and also holds a Japanese example made around 1800–1889. These objects from different regions preserve different forms of fish shapes, painting and carving, showing handmade details in instruments for chanting.

The fish form carries a meaning of vigilance in a Buddhist context. The museum records the idea that fish do not sleep, used to remind practitioners to remain aware and attentive. Its sound originally accompanies sutra chanting. Here you experience a moment of gentle striking and listening. Tap the wooden fish and let mallet sounds meet their resonance. After at least twelve gentle strikes, you can continue listening or select "Finish", leaving this time for your own breathing and thoughts.
scene.celtic-folk-spring.narrative.e0f49:
A spring is enclosed by a low rim and greenery, with a small golden token resting nearby and tiny points of light floating above the surface. Pause at the rim with a bow, then gently place the token onto the water, observing the ripples and light around where it lands. When the actions end, the water remains before you; there is no need to turn away at once.

"A Thought by the Spring" is an imagined spring landscape designed for an everyday pause, joining bending down, setting something aside and quietly watching into a brief rest. You can give the token a personal meaning: something to put down for now, a word not yet spoken, or simply attention to the water's colour. You may watch quietly to the end or leave a reflection to remember the pause.
scene.theravada-water.narrative.e6f585e1:
A water jug, clear water and flower petals form a simple small scene. Hold the jug and drag up and down, letting water flow onto the open surface. Then place a petal on the water and watch it accompany the ripples, finishing with a palms-together gesture of respect. A shallow basin holds the water, while the fine stream from the spout and the soft petals form different lines that your eyes can follow.

This contemporary scene, with clear water and petals as its subject, joins pouring, placing and greeting into a quiet moment. As water and petals meet before you, you may think of gratitude and cherishing, or simply notice the direction of the water and the petal's position. Its meaning at the end comes from your own feelings and needs no single explanation.
scene.tanzaku-tanabata.narrative.733e5ea:
At Tanabata, writing wishes on coloured tanzaku paper strips and tying them to bamboo branches is a familiar festive sight in many parts of Japan. Tanabata in Sendai, Miyagi Prefecture, has clear evidence from the Edo period. Date Masamune left poems related to it, and later notes record night scenes of coloured paper and bamboo decorations. Star worship and hopes for progress in skills and learning gradually acquired local character in the city's festival.

Among the seven kinds of Sendai Tanabata decorations, tanzaku are particularly associated with progress in study and calligraphy. Words on light paper make wishes visible on bamboo branches in streets shared by people's daily lives, while other decorations have meanings of their own. Pick up a tanzaku strip and hang it at the tie on a bamboo branch. You may also leave a wish of your own and quietly watch the paper sway.
scene.yeondeunghoe.narrative.a802a006:
Yeondeunghoe is a Korean lantern festival held around the Buddha's birthday. Temples and local Buddhist communities make and hang coloured lanterns and carry them into the streets. Their light is connected with the Buddhist teaching of moving from ignorance towards wisdom. People also pray for peace for themselves, their families, neighbours and society. Korea's heritage organisation traces it to records of lantern festivals in the Silla period, while new lantern shapes and materials have continued to emerge throughout its long transmission.

Today's Yeondeunghoe is open to people of different ages, backgrounds and faiths. Lantern-making lessons and collective processions allow more people to take part. The lotus is only one of the festival's many lantern forms. Gently touch this lotus lantern and watch the light in the picture slowly move upwards, letting the brightness of one lantern awaken an image of a sea of festival lights.
scene.furin-wind-chime.narrative.3185e45:
Ofusa Kannon Temple in Kashihara, Nara Prefecture, Japan, connects summer bell sounds with prayers for passing safely through the season. The temple explains that local fears of summer illness in the past gave rise to visits praying for safety. Today's wind-chime festival began in 2003, using many ringing chimes to express purification from misfortune and a sense of coolness. Their sound has thus become a distinctive part of summer visits to the temple.

Glass wind chimes also have a side rooted in everyday craft. Accounts of Tokyo's Edo wind chimes describe hand blowing, painting on the inside and the structure in which a hanging paper strip catches the wind to produce sound. In this temple's summer activities, the chimes' clear notes accompany prayers for peace, while glass and paper make a breeze audible. Gently brush the paper strip or tap the bell, listening to a soft chime with a wish for safety, then quietly hear its resonance.
scene.shinto-torii.narrative.cf281d65:
At Japanese shrines, a torii marks the boundary between the shrine grounds and everyday space. The Association of Shinto Shrines' guide to worship treats the whole precinct as a sacred place. Before passing through the torii, people often pause and bow, then walk along the approach towards the deity. This brief pause is connected with respect for the deity and the place, giving entry to the grounds a rhythm different from ordinary passage.

An actual shrine visit may also include purification with water and reverence before the worship hall, and each shrine has practices of its own. A bow before the torii is one expression of respect when moving from everyday life into the precinct. Approach the torii, gently bow your head and stand quietly before the courtyard, letting your gaze turn from outside the gate towards the still shrine grounds.
scene.tibetan-wheel.narrative.5f53963f:
Prayer wheels are objects found in Tibetan Buddhist practice in Tibet and the Himalayas. Rolled papers bearing sacred texts and mantras are placed inside a cylinder that turns clockwise around its axis. The wheel is connected with reciting mantras, prayer and the intention to benefit all beings, and is particularly associated with devotion to Avalokiteshvara. Museum research includes examples of mantra scrolls from around the twelfth to thirteenth centuries. The rolled texts and turning body preserve historical evidence of this practice.

Prayer wheels range from small portable objects to large wheels beside monasteries and pilgrimage paths. Both monastics and lay devotees may use them in daily life or on devotional visits. Before you is a fixed wheel by a covered walkway. Gently swipe its body to set it turning clockwise, then watch it slowly stop, standing quietly for a moment amid the last movement.
scene.slavic-wreath.narrative.32204be5:
In Kupala midsummer customs in parts of Ukraine, young people gather outside the village to sing, take part in activities around fires and weave crowns of grasses and flowers. Connected with ideas about summer vegetation, water and fire, the festival later became interwoven with the Christian feast of Saint John. Medieval texts already record related festivities, while later communities preserved their own distinctive songs, bonfires and wreath customs.

Young women placed wreaths on the water and watched the direction of their drift as a way of divining love, marriage and the future. Some places in Poland also have similar midsummer wreath customs, with differing details. Slowly weave the flowers and grasses together, gently place the wreath on the water and watch it drift away. Hold onto the feeling of midsummer; its path on the water does not answer a person's future.
scene.crane.narrative.ce3adcb8:
In Hiroshima's culture of peace remembrance in Japan, paper cranes are closely connected with the story of Sadako Sasaki. Sadako experienced the atomic bombing at age two. Hospitalised with leukaemia in 1955, she folded paper cranes hoping to recover, and died in October of the same year. Through this particular life story, paper cranes carry remembrance of the children who suffered from the atomic bombing.

Her friends began a memorial campaign, and people from many places later offered paper cranes to the Children's Peace Monument, extending personal care into a shared hope for peace. Hiroshima City still tells the story of Sadako's crane-folding today, connecting the wish to live with a commitment to cherishing peace in remembrance. Fold the neck, tail and wings step by step, lift a paper crane and, if you wish, leave a message for peace of your own.
scene.lantern.narrative.388254dc:
Bamboo ribs support thin paper, and the lantern hangs from a wooden frame, with a small wooden plaque waiting below. Light the paper lantern and warm light gradually glows through its shade. Move the plaque beneath it, joining fine cord and lantern, and the light remains with the plaque before you. The lantern neither rises into the sky nor floats away on water; this moment of companionship stays close by.

"A Lantern Beneath the Moon" creates a contemporary scene for everyday wishes, joining lighting a lamp, hanging a plaque and quiet observation into a pause with a beginning and end. The plaque can hold a wish for family, friends or yourself, or remain blank. People need not understand the lantern in the same way: some want to remember a wish, while others simply like the paper glowing. After hanging the plaque, watch quietly for a moment and let this round come to rest in soft light.
